column4: 3 Checklist 3 (no lost error; failures reported where they happen) and rule 4 (restic-bko parity): restic-bko's setLateFlags, internal/fs/flags_linux.go:181-213 at 12a275f62, ignores xattrUnsupported from setCompression and joins every error (errors.Join)
column6: restore_flags_with's btrfs-compression path handles errors differently from restic-bko in two ways. First, a btrfs.compression that the target file system can't hold (EOPNOTSUPP) becomes a per-file error, where restic-bko ignores it. Second, `set_first.and(set_property).and(set_late)` keeps only the first of three errors, where restic-bko joins all three. So a real failure to set i or a is dropped behind a once-per-kind Unsupported warning. set_compression also runs even when `own | first == current`. restic-bko sets the property again only beside its FS_IOC_SETFLAGS.
column7: (a) Take a btrfs tree under a directory with `btrfs property set <dir> compression zstd`. Its children inherit btrfs.compression and flag c. Restore it onto ext4, which keeps FS_COMPR_FL. set_first succeeds and set_compression fails with EOPNOTSUPP. path_error turns that into a plain String error of kind Unsupported, so it is not counted, but warn_restore dedupes only the Unsupported struct. Every such file therefore warns 'restore F: set btrfs.compression of F: Operation not supported (os error 95)'. restic-bko prints nothing. (b) Take the same kind of snapshot with a c+i file and restore it onto XFS as euid 0 inside a user namespace, with no CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE in the initial namespace. XFS refuses FS_COMPR_FL, so set_first returns Unsupported linux.inode_flags 0x4, warned once and not counted. set_late's FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR fails with EPERM, and `.and()` discards that error. The file comes back without immutable, with no warning naming it and no exit-1 count. restic-bko reports the joined EPERM. The unit test restore_flags_compression_on_zfs_xflags asserts the divergent error (`result.is_err() == zfs`).
column8: Collect the three results into RestoreErrors::result(vec) and drop its illumos-only dead_code allow. warn_restore and restore_error_counts already judge each error on its own. Map an xattr_unsupported error from set_compression to Ok, as restic-bko's setCompression does. Call set_compression only inside the `own | first != current` branch. Tests: change the ZFS rows of restore_flags_compression_on_zfs_xflags to expect Ok. Add a row where set_first is Unsupported and add_xflags returns EPERM, and assert that the EPERM survives and counts (restore_error_counts with root true).
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): I could not refute it. The code, the unit tests and a real run on cinqcent all confirm the finding. **Code (rustic_core ead8a63).** linux.rs:961 sends any set_compression error through path_error. At :983, `set_first.and(set_property).and(set_late)` returns only the first of the three errors. set_compression is called whether or not `own | first == current`. restic-bko at 12a275f62 does three things differently in flags_linux.go: - setCompression returns nil when xattrUnsupported says the error is unsupported. - setLateFlags appends every error and joins them, and restoreFlagsWith joins again. - The property is set again only inside `if own|want != current`. Its test says "Only i to add: no SETFLAGS, no property", while rustic's test expects ["compression zstd", "xflags 0x8"]. warn_restore dedupes only the Unsupported and SidUnmapped structs, so a String error is warned once per file. **Run.** I used rel11's ~/backotter-work/bko-bin/linux binaries. That rustic-bko was built from rustic_core a04257f, and `git diff a04257f ead8a63` does not touch linux.rs, osattrs.rs or restore.rs. The restic-bko is 12a275f62. The source was a btrfs directory with `btrfs property set ... compression zstd`, holding f1 (c) and f2 (c+i). Both tools backed it up as m, then restored it onto ext4 and XFS loop mounts in /mnt/bko-ram, under a `cmp-run.sh --reserve 1 1`. rustic-bko ran with `--strict-exit`. - **(a) ext4, as root.** Both tools warn once per entry from the xattr step. rustic-bko then prints a second warning for each of the 3 entries, such as `[WARN] restore cdir/f1: set btrfs.compression of W/me/rustic-root/cdir/f1: Not supported (os error 95)`. Both exit 0, because rustc 1.94.1 maps errno 95 to ErrorKind::Unsupported, so the error is not counted. - **(b) XFS, as uid m and as root in `unshare -U -r`.** f2 comes back without i under both tools. restic-bko prints `ignoring error for /cdir/f2: FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR ...: operation not permitted` and `Fatal: There were 1 errors`, and exits 1. rustic-bko exits 0 and nothing it prints mentions f2's immutable flag; it gives only the once-per-kind `linux.inode_flags 0x4 not supported` warning. - **ext4, as m and in a user namespace.** Same as (b): the EPERM is hidden behind the btrfs.compression warning. rustic-bko exits 0, restic-bko exits 1. On any target other than btrfs, set_property always fails, so set_late's error is always dropped there. **Not upstream.** git blame -w -M -C gives every line of restore_flags_with to backotter commits (fcac5fa, 6ff672d, eb6371b, 555955e, 02b3f90), and fcac5fa added linux.rs. **No rule wins.** - Rule 3: the fix stays in our files, linux.rs and our RestoreErrors in osattrs.rs. - Rule 4: there is no repository change, and the fix moves rustic-bko toward restic-bko. - Rule 5 covers style fixes; this is a behaviour change, flagged as changing output, so it goes to the user. - The note that cross-tool compat is a courtesy does not save it either. The lost EPERM fails checklist 3 on its own, and rustic-bko's restore_error_counts and `--strict-exit` comments promise to count what restic-bko counts. **Severity.** S2 stays: this is error handling, and the restored trees are identical under both tools. S1 is not warranted because the exit status differs only in non-root or user-namespace restores. **Nuances.** - (a)'s "restic-bko prints nothing" is true of the flags step only: restic-bko still prints its xattr-step warning per file. - The text is musl's "Not supported", not "Operation not supported". - (b) also happens as a plain non-root user, without a user namespace. **Fix-sketch nits.** - RestoreErrors::result's allow should widen to `not(any(target_os = "illumos", target_os = "linux"))`, not be dropped, because the function is still unused on BSD and Haiku. - Moving set_compression into the branch also changes the `(COMPR, COMPR|FS_IMMUTABLE_FL, zstd)` row of restore_flags_keep_btrfs_compression to ["xflags 0x8"]. The sketch doesn't list that row. The scratch directory on cinqcent is removed, with nothing left mounted and no loop devices. No repository was changed.

column6: os_preallocate calls libc::fallocate with libc::off_t. On 32-bit glibc (i686/armv7 -linux-gnu, which cfg(target_os = "linux") admits) that type is 32 bits, so `off_t::try_from(len)` fails for any len over 2 GiB. sparse::lseek switched to the 64-bit call for exactly this reason. fill_holes and preallocate both go through os_preallocate.
column7: Build for i686-unknown-linux-gnu and restore a 3 GiB swap file that an interrupted restore left with holes. fill_holes calls allocate_holes, which calls os_preallocate, and that returns 'out of range integral type conversion attempted'. This is not EOPNOTSUPP/ENOSYS, so cannot_allocate doesn't absorb it. FilledHoles.error is set, the holes stay and swapon refuses the file. preallocate of any file over 2 GiB is skipped with only a debug line. No shipped build (64-bit, musl) is affected.
column8: On target_env gnu (and musl, for symmetry) call libc::fallocate64 with off64_t, behind the same cfg alias sparse::lseek uses, ideally one shared alias. Test: a fill_holes run on a sparse file over 2 GiB where TMPDIR allows, on a 32-bit gnu cross build if one is ever made.
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): Confirmed at rustic_core ead8a63. I could not refute it. OURS: osattrs.rs was added whole by fcac5fa (backotter:), and lines 745-765 blame to 6ff672d, ed28fe0 and dd1a67b, all backotter: commits. HEADERS: Debian glibc 2.41-12+deb13u4, /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/fcntl-linux.h:425-439, declares fallocate(int, int, __off_t, __off_t). It redirects to fallocate64(__off64_t) only under __USE_FILE_OFFSET64. In bits/typesizes.h, __OFF_T_TYPE (line 51) is __SYSCALL_SLONG_TYPE, which lines 30-34 set to __SLONGWORD_TYPE except on x32; bits/types.h:113 makes that long int, so 32 bits on i386 and arm. libc 0.2.189 (both Cargo.locks): - gnu/b32/mod.rs:60 makes off_t i32 unless --cfg libc_unstable_gnu_time_bits="64" is set (build.rs:179-218, default 32; the forks never set it). - linux/mod.rs:3527-3528 links fallocate64 only under gnu_file_offset_bits64. - android/mod.rs:23 makes off_t c_long; uclibc arm and mips32 are 32-bit too; musl/mod.rs:33 makes it i64. - So the binding matches the header. There is no layout error and no UB: the defect is the range the call can take. MEASURED on Copland (nightly-2026-10-31, -Zbuild-std, offline, libc =0.2.189): - off_t is 4 bytes on i686-unknown-linux-gnu, armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf, i686-linux-android and armv7-linux-androideabi. It is 8 bytes on i686-unknown-linux-musl and x86_64-gnu. - readelf shows libc::fallocate as UND fallocate (the non-LFS symbol) on all of them. - `cargo check -p rustic_core --lib` at ead8a63 passes for i686-gnu, armv7-gnueabihf and i686-android. So those builds exist and the path is reachable. - i32::try_from(3<<30).map_err(io::Error::other) gives kind Other, raw_os_error None and 'out of range integral type conversion attempted'. cannot_allocate (sparse.rs:765-767) therefore does not absorb it. - A failing fstatfs gives no escape either: allocates_on and fills_holes_on use is_none_or, so they default to true. PATH: as stated. restore.rs:802-816 warns 'holes not filled' and counts the file unchanged, while --dry-run counts it modified. WORSE THAN STATED: an existing file over 2 GiB that the restore writes into (Modify, not fresh) depends on set_length's preallocate (local_destination.rs:741-743, via files_writer.rs:195) to allocate holes that zero blobs matched. That error only reaches the debug log (osattrs.rs:740-742), and fill_holes runs only for Existing and Verified files (restore.rs:825 and 868). So those holes stay with no warning. NO RULE WINS: - The code is in our own files, so rule 3 is not engaged. - Neither the repository nor the nodes change (rule 4). restic-bko already passes int64 offsets through unix.Fallocate (fillholes.go:92, preallocate_linux.go:25), so the fix restores parity. - Rules 1, 2 and 5 are holt's. - BACKOTTER.md:1416-1420 states the 32-bit glibc/Android off_t intent for lseek64, so this is drift from the fork's own design. S2 AS IN R2-02: build-backotter.sh:51-53 refuses *-linux-gnu, and nothing builds Android, so no shipped or tested binary is affected. It is not S3, because no lint names it. changes_output false: glibc x86_64 exports fallocate64 at the address of fallocate (Debian 2.41, 0x1046f0), and libc's musl fallocate64 is a wrapper around fallocate (musl/lfs64.rs:10-17). NOTES FOR F11: - fallocate64 exists in libc 0.2.189 for gnu and uclibc (linux/mod.rs:3826-3828), for musl (lfs64.rs) and for Android (android/mod.rs:3627). - The lseek alias cfg (sparse.rs:466-469) leaves 32-bit uclibc with a 32-bit off_t for both calls. - A compile-time size assert on the alias, checked by a cross check build with -Zbuild-std, is a test the farm can run. Scratch dirs removed on Cinqcent, on Copland and in the local scratchpad.

column6: restore_acls never removes an ACL the node lacks (`let Some(acl) = ... else { return; }`, line 392), and restore_system_extattrs (359) never removes a system extattr the node lacks. Meanwhile exact.rs same_generic_attributes counts an attribute the file has and a BackOtter node lacks as a difference (known_bko). So `restore --exact` on FreeBSD/NetBSD keeps ACL entries the snapshot never granted, and it never converges.
column7: FreeBSD 15 UFS mounted `-o acls` (or NetBSD FFSv2ea `posix1eacls`). Back up /data, where f is 0660 with no extended ACL, so its node has no freebsd.acl_access. Then run `setfacl -m u:mallory:rw f` and `setfacl -d -m u:mallory:r /data/d`, and then `rustic restore --exact snap /data`. now has freebsd.acl_access and freebsd.acl_default, the node has neither, and the snapshot is BackOtter's, so same_generic_attributes says the metadata differs and the metadata pass runs: chmod 0660 sets the POSIX.1e mask to rw, and restore_acls returns without touching the ACL. mallory keeps rw on f, and new files in d still inherit u:mallory:r. The restore reports success. Every later --exact run sees the same difference and sets the metadata again, which moves ctime each time, against BACKOTTER.md's promise. The same happens with NFSv4 ACLs on ZFS with aclmode=passthrough, and with system extattrs added after the backup. On Linux the same case works, because POSIX ACLs are system.posix_acl_* xattrs and set_xattrs_all removes the ones the node lacks; the BSDs are the outlier. restic-bko's nodeRestoreACLs (internal/fs/attrs_bsd.go:260-275, `if !ok { return }`) has the same gap, so parity holds today, but both forks are wrong.
column8: Pass known_bko through os::restore_acls and os::restore_attributes, as restore_attributes already takes it. In a BackOtter snapshot, for each ACL type the file system has (the same lpathconf test fill_acls uses), give a node that lacks one the trivial form: set the 3-entry access ACL from the mode, delete the default ACL with __acl_delete_link(ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT) (a libc symbol on FreeBSD and on NetBSD 10), and set nfs4_trivial_acl(mode) for NFSv4. Likewise remove system extattrs the node lacks, leaving out UFS_ACL_EXTATTRS. Fix restic-bko's attrs_bsd.go the same way. Test: a freebsd15 UFS-acls guest and a netbsd11 FFSv2ea guest do the setfacl case above; after one --exact, getfacl shows no extended ACL, and a second --exact changes nothing (same ctime). Then run the four-direction cross-restore.
column9: confirmed (S1->S1): I could not refute it. Code reading and two live runs both reproduce the failure. All the cited code is ours, so the finding is in scope. A backotter: commit added each file whole: freebsd_netbsd.rs and netbsd.rs (337df0a), exact.rs (979248b), freebsd.rs and osattrs.rs (fcac5fa). scope-rustic_core.txt lists them as added. LIVE TEST: rel11's rustic-bko (rustic_core a04257f). Between a04257f and ead8a63 the only changes are a closure rename and formatting, so it is the same code. Each OS ran in a throwaway guest-run.sh guest on cinqcent under cmp-run.sh --reserve 1 5, WEAR_TAG audit:forkaudit-f10:F4-01. Scratch files are removed. - FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE-p6, md UFS mounted acls,noatime: - Control: --exact twice over the matching tree moved no ctime. - After `setfacl -m u:mallory:rw f` and a default ACL on d, a new backup records freebsd.acl_access on f and freebsd.acl_default on d. The snapshot has neither. - `RUSTIC_STRICT_EXIT=true restore --numeric-id --exact` exits 0 with no warnings. f still has user:mallory:rw- with mask::rw-, mode -rw-rw----, and d keeps its default ACL. - Runs #2 and #3 each moved the ctimes of f and d. A file created in d afterwards inherited user:mallory:r--. - `setextattr system bkotest hello c` survives --exact, and c's ctime moves on every run. - ZFS with aclmode=passthrough: same result. mallory's NFSv4 entries stay and the ctimes move on each run. - NetBSD 11.1, FFSv2ea mounted posix1eacls: the same results. netbsd.acl_access/acl_default are recorded, mallory stays after --exact with exit 0, the ctimes of f and d move on run #2, and the system extattr survives. RULES: none wins. - Rule 3: the fix stays in our files, plus one token in our set_metadata hunk. - Rule 4: the change is restore-side only, and node and repository format are unchanged. restic-bko @12a275f has the same gap: nodeRestoreACLs (internal/fs/attrs_bsd.go:260-276, `if !ok { return }`), and sameGenericAttributes (internal/restorer/exact.go:461-483) treats a missing attribute as a difference under fromBackOtter. Parity holds today, and both forks are wrong, as the finding says. - Rule 5: this is a behaviour change, so it goes to the user. That only routes the fix; it does not drop it. - BACKOTTER.md's --exact text ("exactly the snapshot"; a generic attribute the node lacks counts in a BackOtter snapshot "where it was none") contradicts what the restore does. Line ~674 ("as FreeBSD's system extended attributes" are left as they are) will need updating with the fix. CORRECTIONS to the finding: - (a) On FreeBSD 15.1, `setfacl -d -m u:mallory:r d` fails on an empty default ACL ("acl_calc_mask() failed: Invalid argument"). The repro needs `setfacl -d -m u::rwx,g::rx,o::rx,u:mallory:r,m::rx d`. - (b) The NFSv4 case only fails where chmod keeps extra entries (ZFS aclmode=passthrough, and presumably restricted). - With ZFS's default aclmode=discard, the restore's chmod dropped mallory's entries and --exact converged after one run, with no ctime moved on run #2. - NetBSD FFSv2ea mounted nfs4acls behaved the same way. - Linux's case was checked by reading the code only: set_xattrs_all removes the system.posix_acl_* xattrs a node lacks. - (c) Notes for the fixer: - NetBSD's __acl_delete_link is syscall 489 (sys/kern/syscalls.master trunk: 487 get_link, 488 set_link, 489 delete_link, 499 lpathconf; 487/488/499 match ours and worked on 11.1). The module calls these by number, so 489 can be used the same way. - Treating a missing attribute as "none" also covers attributes the backup could not read: R3-02's EPERM/EACCES-as-none, and fill_system_extattrs recording nothing for a non-root backup. A root --exact restore of a non-root snapshot would then strip system extattrs. Decide that together with R3-02.

column4: checklist 1 (FFI constants proved against the platform headers, file and version cited); smallest unsafe (Rustonomicon) (prior: R3-05)
column6: I checked R3-05's numbers against the headers, and they are right. NetBSD's libc also exports the three calls by name, so netbsd_sys's raw libc::syscall wrappers aren't needed.
column7: Nothing is wrong today. The values match: SYS___acl_get_link 487, SYS___acl_set_link 488 and SYS_lpathconf 499 in NetBSD sys/sys/syscall.h on both netbsd-10 and netbsd-11 (lines 1369, 1372 and 1405, generated from syscalls.master 1.316). _PC_ACL_EXTENDED is 14 and _PC_ACL_NFS4 is 17 in sys/sys/unistd.h on netbsd-10 and netbsd-11 (lines 215 and 222). NetBSD 10's lib/libc/sys/Makefile.inc builds `__acl_get_link.S __acl_set_link.S` (line 96) and `lpathconf.S` (line 130), so the symbols exist, as freebsd_sys already uses them. Calling by number keeps three `unsafe fn`s with no # Safety (R3-04), and a wrong number would call another syscall with pointer arguments.
column8: Drop netbsd_sys's syscall wrappers. Use one `unsafe extern "C"` block, with link_name __acl_get_link, __acl_set_link and lpathconf, for both FreeBSD and NetBSD, and keep only `OS` per system. In freebsd_acl.rs and BACKOTTER.md:109-112, cite the headers above. This also closes R3-04. Check `nm -D /usr/lib/libc.so | grep acl_get_link` on netbsd11 before relying on it.

column4: checklist 6 (duplication between modules); Effective Rust (one implementation per behaviour)
column6: clear_restricting_flags is written four times: freebsd.rs:271, netbsd.rs:91, openbsd.rs:98 and dragonfly.rs:84. Each is lstat, mask with RESTRICTING, then lchflags/chflagsat. bsd_held.rs already has this logic once (RESTRICTING picked per OS at 23-28, set_path_flags at 52), and the copies have drifted.
column7: They have already drifted. OpenBSD's copy calls its own extern chflagsat (openbsd.rs:26), while bsd_held uses libc::chflagsat on the same target. Its error says 'chflagsat', while bsd_held's by-path step on OpenBSD says 'lchflags' (R3-16). A change to which flags count as restricting, or to how they are cleared, has to be made in five places. If one copy is missed, the plain and held clears disagree on that OS: the plain clear leaves a flag on, and the rename or unlink that follows fails with EPERM.
column8: Add `pub(super) fn clear_restricting_flags(path)` to bsd_held.rs: symlink_metadata, return if nothing is restricting, then set_path_flags(path, flags & !RESTRICTING). Have the four OS modules re-export it with `pub(super) use super::bsd_held::clear_restricting_flags;` and delete their copies, plus openbsd.rs's extern block (R3-15).
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): Confirmed at rustic_core ead8a63, but part of the failure case is overstated. I changed nothing and ran no host test: the code, libc's source and the OS headers settle the question, and booting four BSD guests would add nothing. The duplication is real and the code is ours. `git blame -w -M -C` gives all four plain copies to ccc68a2 (backotter:, 2026-11-01): freebsd.rs:271, netbsd.rs:91, openbsd.rs:98, dragonfly.rs:84. Each one does `symlink_metadata`, returns if `flags & RESTRICTING == 0`, then sets `flags & !RESTRICTING` by path. b660a71 (backotter:, 2026-11-14) then added bsd_held.rs. It wrote the same sequence a fifth time (lines 66-67, then set_path_flags at 52-61 on the by-path tail at 95-96) and mapped each OS to its mask a second time (lines 23-28), instead of reusing the copies. Our own code already does this once elsewhere: linux.rs builds its plain and held clears on one function, clear_restricting_open (735 and 764). restic-bko's restrictflags_bsd.go also keeps both in one file around one setFlagsOf. No behaviour has drifted today, on any target. The FFI checks: - **FreeBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly:** both paths call `libc::lchflags(p, (flags & !R).into())`. libc 0.2.189 declares it with `c_ulong` (freebsdlike/mod.rs:1557, netbsd/mod.rs:1915). I checked the crate's sha256, 3eaf3ede..., against both Cargo.locks. That matches `int lchflags(const char *, unsigned long)` in FreeBSD releng/15.0 sys/sys/stat.h:384, NetBSD netbsd-11 stat.h v1.70:267 and DragonFly 6.4 stat.h:320. - **OpenBSD:** openbsd.rs's own extern (26-33) and libc's (openbsd/mod.rs:1931) both declare chflagsat with `flags: c_uint`. Both match OpenBSD sys/stat.h v1.29:216, `int chflagsat(int, const char *, unsigned int, int)`. AT_FDCWD (-100) and AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW (0x02) match fcntl.h v1.23:209,212, so both paths make the same call. - **Flag bits:** they match bsd_flags.rs on all four systems. NetBSD's header marks UF_NOUNLINK and SF_NOUNLINK as NOT IMPLEMENTED, and OpenBSD has no such flags. Both errors only reach `debug!` (osattrs.rs:456 and 609). The drift the finding cites is in text only, and the ledger already has both items as S3s: R3-15 (the extra extern) and R3-16 (the wrong label). In that pair, openbsd.rs's 'chflagsat' is the correct label and bsd_held's 'lchflags' is the wrong one. The overstated part: changing which flags count as restricting is not five edits. It is one edit in bsd_flags.rs (lines 48-66), and the restricting_flags test pins it. The failure can still happen through ordinary maintenance, in two ways: - **A per-OS mask change.** Giving one OS its own set means changing both bsd_held's alias and that module's import. If the bsd_held alias is missed, it still compiles, because NETBSD_OPENBSD stays for NetBSD. The plain and held clears then quietly disagree, which is the finding's failure. - **A change to the call.** The by-path call exists in five functions and has already diverged once: b660a71 chose libc::chflagsat and a new label, while openbsd.rs kept its own extern. No rule wins. The lines are ours, and the fix stays inside our files, so rule 3 is kept. It is restore-side only, with no change to the repository or to nodes, so rule 4 is kept. The only output change is a debug label. RA5 lists duplicated logic as S2, and the ledger confirmed the same kind of finding as S2 before: R5-05, H8-05 and H8-11. The fix sketch has these gaps: 1. openbsd.rs's extern block can't simply be deleted, because restore_file_flags's symlink branch (openbsd.rs:81) also calls it. Switch that call to `libc::chflagsat` in the same commit. 2. Drop the RESTRICTING imports that become unused (freebsd.rs:25, netbsd.rs:11, openbsd.rs:8, dragonfly.rs:10), and move the function's doc comment to bsd_held.rs with it. 3. Fix R3-16's per-OS label in set_path_flags in the same commit. Otherwise OpenBSD's plain-clear debug text changes from the correct 'chflagsat' to 'lchflags'. 4. The re-export `pub(super) use super::bsd_held::clear_restricting_flags;` is legal, because it has the same `pub(in osattrs)` visibility as the item. 5. None of this compiles on Linux, so F12 needs the build round on all four BSDs.

column4: clippy::multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block; checklist 6 (the same behaviour on every BSD) (prior: R3-12)
column6: This restates R3-12 with a wider fix. OpenBSD's restore_file_flags uses chflags(2), which follows symlinks, for every type but a symlink. The other three BSDs use lchflags for every type, and chflagsat(AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW) alone would do on OpenBSD, which also leaves the block one unsafe op.
column7: If a path the restore made as a regular file or directory is replaced by a symlink before the late flags pass, OpenBSD alone sets the node's flags (for example schg) on the symlink's target. Upstream's set_permissions follows symlinks too, so this is consistency, not a new hole. It is also the only multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block hit in the unit (F1, OpenBSD).
column8: Call chflagsat(AT_FDCWD, p, bits, AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW) for every type, with one unsafe block and its SAFETY comment, and drop the `symlink` variable. Use libc::chflagsat (R3-15).

column4: checklist 3 (nothing lost silently); checklist 2 (input from the file system)
column6: extattr_read asks for the size, then reads into a buffer of that size. extattr_get_link(2) and extattr_list_link(2) return the bytes copied and give no ERANGE when the buffer is too small. So a system extattr that grows between the two calls is stored truncated, and a list that grows loses its last name (list_names stops at a cut-short name). No warning is given either way.
column7: This can only happen in a race. The backup runs as root on FreeBSD UFS or ZFS, and another process rewrites system.foo from 10 to 20 bytes between the size query and the read. The node keeps the first 10 bytes, and the restore writes that truncated value. On UFS (ffs_getextattr) and ZFS (zfs_getextattr_sa/_dir), uiomove copies min(resid, size).
column8: When the read returns exactly `size` bytes, query the size again. If it grew, retry with the new size, a few times at most, then fail. Do this together with R3-19: have the size query return usize, not a zeroed Vec.

column4: checklist 2 (input from the system: what statfs reports)
column6: on_zfs decides ZFS by f_fstypename == "zfs" (fs_type, 202). Through a nullfs mount of a ZFS dataset, f_fstypename is "nullfs", but the files still carry ZFS's flags, so freebsd_file_flags and open_for_attrs treat ZFS files as UFS.
column7: I haven't checked this on a guest; it is likely. Picture a backup inside a FreeBSD jail, or of a Bastille or iocage thin jail, where the data is a nullfs mount of a ZFS dataset. Every file then keeps freebsd.file_flags=0x800 (archive alone, which ZFS gives every file), so each node gets an extra attribute. A file whose archive bit was cleared (flags 0) gets None, and ZFS sets the bit again on restore. ZFS project IDs are skipped, because open_for_attrs requires on_zfs. restic-bko does the same (internal/fs/flags_freebsd.go:65), so parity holds.
column8: On the freebsd15 guest, check what statfs and FSGETXATTR report through nullfs. If ZFS's ioctls pass through, decide ZFS by whether ZFS_IOC_FSGETXATTR succeeds (it fails with ENOTTY on UFS), or treat nullfs as its lower file system. Change both forks together. This changes what a backup records, so it goes to the user first.

column3: crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/illumos.rs:964 (restore_one_xattr_meta's fchownat; reached from osattrs::restore_attributes, called for every node at restore.rs:1730 whatever ownership(opts) says)
column4: Checklist 2 (no wrong result on real input) and 4; API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR; rule 4 (cross-restore). A privacy issue, so RA5 S1
column6: Each extended attribute's owner and group are restored as the snapshot's raw numbers, whatever the restore's ownership mode. With --no-ownership the attributes are still chowned. With the default by-name mode the file gets its owner by name, while its attributes get the backup host's numbers.
column7: (a) Root on illumos runs `rustic restore --no-ownership` of a snapshot taken on another host. The restored files stay owned by root, but each attribute file is fchownat'd to the snapshot's uid/gid, say 1001:1001, which on this host may be another user. That user then owns, and with mode 0600 can read, attribute data of a file they have no access to. Run as non-root, the same fchownat fails with EPERM, and tally.io prints a warning for every file that has attributes. (b) A default (by-name) restore onto a host where alice is uid 1500, while the backup host had her as 1001 and 1001 is bob here. set_user_group gives the file 1500 (alice), and restore_xattr_meta gives its attributes 1001 (bob). restic-bko restores everything by number (restoreXattrMeta in xattrmeta_illumos.go), so the two tools' results differ here as well. Found by reading restore.rs:1703-1731 and illumos.rs:920-999; not run on a guest.
column8: Pass the restore's Ownership, or the uid/gid the file itself was just given, into osattrs::restore_attributes and on to restore_xattr_meta. Skip fchownat for Ownership::None. For ByName (and Numeric), give an attribute whose snapshot uid/gid equals the node's meta.uid/gid the owner the file got; others keep their number. Test on the guest: restore with --no-ownership as root, then check that an attribute's owner is unchanged (root), not the snapshot's uid. This is a behaviour change, so it goes to the user (rule 5, D3).
column9: confirmed (S1->S1): I could not refute it. A guest run showed the failure, and only one side claim, about restic-bko parity, is wrong. CODE (rustic_core ead8a63). illumos.rs:964 calls fchownat with meta.uid and meta.gid unconditionally. Only ENOENT is skipped. - osattrs::restore_attributes (osattrs.rs:1235) takes (path, node, known_bko) and has no ownership parameter. There is no global ownership state either: I grepped for statics and atomics. - restore.rs:1730 calls it for every node. ownership(opts) gates only the file's own chown and restore_owner (restore.rs:1704-1715). - The lines are ours. illumos.rs was added by backotter commits fcac5fa/2c52ef2; blame of 949-999 gives 2c52ef2, c442156 and one more backotter commit. The call is our hunk. RUN. I ran omnios58 (OmniOS r151058) on Cinqcent, through guest-run.sh under cmp-run.sh --reserve, with roundrel11's illumos binaries. Those are rustic 9ddbbaf / rustic_core a04257f. The diff a04257f..ead8a63 is rustfmt and docs only in illumos.rs, illumos_xattrmeta.rs and bsd_extattr.rs, so the behaviour is the same as at ead8a63/3853eb3. The source files and their attribute 'note' were 1001:1001, mode 0600. - (a) Root, --no-ownership: file 0:0, file@note 1001:1001, for both files. - Control, --numeric-id: everything 1001:1001. - (b) alice renumbered 1001->1500, bob added as 1001, then a default (by-name) restore: file 1500:1500, note 1001:1001 (bob). - Who can read it: bob could not read root's 0600 restored file. He did read its attribute through libc's exported __openattrdirat, and he overwrote it; root then read back 'written-by-bob'. Where the base file was 0644, plain runat was enough. Control: for a root-owned 0600 attribute, bob got EACCES. - Why, per illumos-gate: - copen()'s FXATTRDIROPEN only looks the base file up (usr/src/uts/common/syscall/open.c). - zfs_zaccess() checks an xattr directory against the base file's ACE_READ_NAMED_ATTRS (usr/src/uts/common/fs/zfs/zfs_acl.c). - acl_trivial_access_masks() always gives that bit to everyone@ (usr/src/common/acl/acl_common.c). - __openattrdirat is exported (libc/port/mapfile-vers, SUNWprivate_1.1). - So the attribute file's own owner and mode are the only guard, and the restore gives it to whoever has the snapshot's number on this host. - (c) carol, non-root, --no-ownership: one warning per file with attributes, '[WARN] restore file: fchownat /f5/c/dst/file/@note: Not owner (os error 1)', exit 0, not counted. RULES. None beats it. The change is restore-only: no node or repository format changes, and cross-restore is unaffected (rule 4). Rule 5 makes it a decision for the user (D3), as the finding says. CORRECTION. The finding says the two tools' results differ. They don't, in equivalent modes. restic-bko's restoreXattrMeta (internal/fs/xattrmeta_illumos.go) also ignores ownershipByName. - Observed: restic-bko --ownership-by-name gave exactly rustic-bko's by-name result (file 1500, note 1001). - restic-bko's default numeric restore equals rustic --numeric-id. - The defaults differ only in the file's own owner, from stock's defaults. - So a fix in rustic alone makes the forks' by-name restores diverge. restic-bko needs the same change, which is out of ForkAudit1's scope and the user's call. restic has no --no-ownership. FIX NOTES. 1. With Ownership::None, skip fchownat. The attribute stays the restorer's and 0600. 2. With ByName, do as the finding proposes. Attributes with other owners keep their numbers, since nodes keep no names for them. 3. exact.rs same_generic_attributes compares illumos.xattr_meta whole, uid and gid included, even when ownership is false. After the fix, --exact --no-ownership would never match a file with attributes, so the comparison must leave out the attribute owners when ownership is off. restic-bko's sameMetadata needs the same. 4. Attribute ACL entries by number are fine: stock tools restore POSIX ACL entries by number in every mode. 5. Add the --no-ownership and renumbered-user checks to testvm/compare/illumos/roundtrip.sh. Log: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-mchobbit-git-backotter/fbac8b1f-8f61-4216-bf95-431973e8cc08/scratchpad/f501/run.log. The Cinqcent scratch and log dirs are removed, and the reservation is released.

column3: crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/illumos.rs:895-896 (read_xattr_meta keeps st_uid/st_gid); illumos_xattrmeta.rs:50-59 (XattrMeta has no SID fields)
column4: Checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); the fork's own rule for SID owners (illumos.rs:391-394, 'Not the number the backup saw: that may be another SID's by now')
column6: The file's own owner and group SIDs are kept (illumos.owner_sid/group_sid), and so are SIDs in the ACL entries of the file and of each attribute. An attribute file's owner and group are kept only as numbers. When those numbers are ephemeral (above MAXUID), a restore after a reboot gives the attribute to whichever SID idmapd has since given that number, or to none.
column7: On an illumos SMB server, a Windows user writes an alternate data stream. It is stored as a named attribute owned by the user's ephemeral uid, say 2147483650. The backup records uid 2147483650 in illumos.xattr_meta. After a reboot, idmapd hands out ephemeral ids from 2^31 again, in the order SIDs are asked for, so 2147483650 can now be another user's SID. The restore fchownat's the stream to that number, so the other user owns it, while the base file correctly gets the original SID through restore_owner. restic-bko's xattrMeta has the same uid/gid-only form, so both forks need the change. From reading the code and idmap's semantics; not run on a guest with SMB.
column8: Add optional owner_sid/group_sid fields to XattrMeta, with serde default and skip_serializing_if None, in both forks. Readers that don't know them ignore them, so rule 4 holds. Fill them in read_xattr_meta with SidNamer::sid when the id is above MAX_UID. At restore, map them with map_sid, giving nobody plus a SidUnmapped warning, exactly as restore_owner does. Test: extend xattr_meta_json with an entry that has SIDs, and an older reader still parses it. This changes the tree JSON and the restored owners, so it goes to the user (D3).
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): I tried to refute it and could not. The failure case happens. Scope: the lines are ours. illumos.rs was added by fcac5fa and illumos_xattrmeta.rs by 2c52ef2, both backotter: commits. git blame -w -M -C gives illumos.rs 876-913 and 949-999 to 2c52ef2, apart from 4 lines of the R4-01 fix. No upstream code is involved. The code at ead8a63: - read_xattr_meta (illumos.rs:894-901) stores st_uid and st_gid as plain numbers. - In that function SidNamer is used only for the ACL entries (sids.aces, line 906). fill_xattr_meta never calls sids.owner for an attribute file. - restore_one_xattr_meta (line 964) calls fchownat(meta.uid, meta.gid) with no map_sid. - The restore order (restore.rs:1704-1731) is: numeric set_uid_gid, then restore_owner (lchown of the base path only), then set_attributes, then restore_xattr_meta. Nothing ever corrects an attribute file's owner. - The fork's own rule is broken. BACKOTTER.md:615-620 says a backup keeps the SID of "every ephemeral owner, group and ACL entry". The map_sid doc (illumos.rs:391-394) says the stored number is never to be used. Kernel semantics, from illumos-gate master: - **Streams are SID-owned.** smb_fsop_create_stream (uts/common/fs/smbsrv/smb_fsops.c) gives each new stream the base file's va_uid/va_gid, set with kcred. A SID-owned file's streams are therefore SID-owned. - **The backup stores the ephemeral number.** zfs_getattr calls zfs_fuid_map_ids, then kidmap_getuidbysid, so fstatat returns the ephemeral uid and the backup stores it. - **chown checks only the current range.** fchownat (uts/common/syscall/chown.c) checks only VALID_UID (sys/cred.h:164). valid_ephemeral_uid (os/cred.c:1176-1186) accepts min_uid < id <= last_uid. - **Numbering restarts each boot.** The range starts over at IDMAP_WK__MAX_UID+1 = 2147483649 (cred.c:123-124, sys/idmap.h:81). idmapd reserves 8192 uids and 8192 gids at startup (cmd/idmap/idmapd/idmapd.c:426-437). Its ephemeral cache is /var/run/idmap/cache.db (idmapd.h:249-251), created afresh each boot. - **ZFS maps the stale number to whoever holds it now.** zfs_fuid_create (fs/zfs/zfs_fuid.c) maps the id with kidmap_getsidbyuid to the SID idmapd now gives that number. When no SID has it, idmapd answers IDMAP_ERR_NOMAPPING (dbutils.c pid2sid_first_pass: "Ephemeral ids cannot be allocated during pid2sid"). ZFS then stores nobody: null domain, POSIX id 60001. - **Both outcomes are silent.** The chown succeeds either way, while the base file at least gets a SidUnmapped warning. - **Outside the valid range it fails with EINVAL.** That happens when idmapd is not running in the restoring boot. The attribute then stays owned by root, because zfs_acl_ids_create gives a new xattr file its creator's cred. So after a reboot with two SID users, A's stream goes to B or to 60001. B is whichever SID got A's old number first in the new boot, possibly during the restore itself through restore_owner's id_of_sid calls. bko-holt bare-metal restores always run in a new boot. The fork's own test missed this. testvm/compare/illumos/roundtrip.sh:38-40 documents exactly these semantics. But its xattr-meta attribute is chowned to 1500:1501 (line 177), so the second-boot --again run never had a SID-owned attribute file. No R4 row covers this. No rule wins: - Rule 3: the fix is in our own files. - Rule 4 holds with optional fields that serde defaults when absent. XattrMeta has no deny_unknown_fields. restic-bko decodes with encoding/json, which ignores unknown fields. Stock tools never parse illumos.xattr_meta. - Rule 5 routes the change to the user. restic-bko has the same gap: xattrMeta in internal/fs/illumos_xattrmeta.go:15-22 holds only uid and gid, and xattrmeta_illumos.go:133 does a plain unix.Fchownat. Both forks need the fix for parity. Corrections to the finding: - The stream gets the base file's owner and group, not necessarily the writer's. Its SID usually equals the base file's owner_sid, but not after a later change of owner. So the fix must keep the stream's own SIDs, as proposed. - "Or to none" means one of two things: nobody, silently, when the number is in the reserved block but unassigned; or an EINVAL error with root left as owner. - At restore, chown straight to the mapped ids. Severity stays S2, not S1: - SMB checks access to a stream against the base file. smb_fsop_access says "Streams authorization should be performed against the unnamed stream", so what SMB clients can do does not change. - The wrong owner shows in local ls/runat and local O_XATTR access, in ZFS userused@/userquota@ accounting, and in restore fidelity. - Reach is AD-joined SMB servers with ephemeral mapping. This matches how the ledger graded XH1-01 and R4-04. The tree JSON and the restored owners both change, so changes_output is true. I settled this from kernel source and did not run it on a guest. No farm work was done, nothing was changed, and the scratch copy was removed.

column4: Checklist 3 (errors: one failure shouldn't lose unrelated data); consistency with the other backends (XattrsRead::unreadable, illumos.rs:727-750)
column6: On Haiku, one attribute whose stat or read fails, or one that 'keeps growing as it's read' (READ_TRIES), fails the whole file. All of its extended attributes, or all of its typed attributes (haiku.attributes), are then dropped with a single warning. illumos and Linux leave only the unreadable attribute out and keep the rest.
column7: A file has BEOS:TYPE (MIMS), a few typed attributes, and one attribute that another program rewrites, larger each time, during the backup (a mail or indexer status attribute), or one that gives EIO from a bad attribute inode. read_attr returns Err after 3 tries, or read_kind's `?` passes the EIO on. kept() then fails, and fill_attributes warns 'ignoring attributes of X' and sets no haiku.attributes. BEOS:TYPE and every other typed attribute of the file are lost from the snapshot. Because the '{}' marker is missing too, an in-place restore leaves the file's current attributes as they are instead of making them the snapshot's. The same happens to its B_XATTR_TYPE attributes through native_xattrs. In the same way, apply() at restore stops before writing anything when stats() fails on one name.
column8: Have read_kind return the unreadable names with their errors alongside the kept map, as XattrsRead does. Have kept() warn for each and keep the rest, and still set haiku.attributes. In stats(), record a failed stat as unreadable rather than returning it with `?`. Test with FakeBfs: a FakeBfs whose read of one name fails (or whose `grow` is always set) still gives the other attributes, and the failing name is reported.
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): I could not refute it. All of these lines are ours: haiku.rs and haiku_attrs.rs were added whole by 5eba94f ("backotter: Haiku, from branch haiku-attrs"), and the warn in osattrs.rs fill() is ours too. I read the code at ead8a63 and checked BFS behaviour against Haiku master sources (bfs/Inode.cpp, Attribute.cpp, kernel_interface.cpp, kernel/fs/vfs.cpp, libroot/os/fs_attr.cpp). Nothing was built or run, because the code path is not in doubt and a test would show nothing new. The code does what the finding says: - stats() at haiku_attrs.rs:112-114 uses `?` on every stat, and it serves both kinds. So a stat error drops both kinds of attribute, which is more than the finding claims. - read_kind at 173-174 uses `?` on read_attr, and read_attr gives Err after READ_TRIES at 145. - kept() at haiku.rs:184-185 passes the error on, so fill_attributes at 255 sets no haiku.attributes, and osattrs.rs:165-167 warns "ignoring attributes of X" and marks the backup incomplete. - native_xattrs passes the error on, and mapper.rs:161-167 stores an empty extended_attributes list. - apply() at 263 stops at `stats(file)?` before any remove or write. The failure can happen on BFS. One correction to the wording: a bad attribute *inode* fails the listing, not the read. AttributeIterator::GetNext loads every attribute inode (Inode.cpp:3576-3584), and bfs_read_attr_dir returns that error, so names() fails for the whole file, with or without the fix. A bad *data block* in an attribute kept in its own inode fails only that attribute's fs_read_attr. That path is Inode::ReadAttribute -> GetAttribute -> ReadAt -> file_cache_read (Inode.cpp:1246-1255, 1745-1748; NeedsFileCache includes IsAttribute). Listing and stat still succeed there, because they need only the inode. On a failing disk, that is exactly the `?` at read_kind:173-174. Large attributes such as vector icons and Tracker data commonly live in their own inodes. The READ_TRIES trigger is practically impossible. Each fs_stat_attr and fs_read_attr opens the attribute separately (vfs.cpp:9970, 10024), so it would take three growths in a row inside two-syscall windows. The EIO trigger is enough on its own. None of our rules wins: - Rule 4: restic-bko doesn't run on Haiku, so there is no parity to keep, and the format is unchanged. - Rule 3: the fix stays in our own files. - The output change goes to the user (D3). - The fork's own documented xattr policy says otherwise (b4337fa; BACKOTTER.md:700-705: "the file's others are kept (stock dropped them all)"). It names Haiku as an exception, "Haiku's are read whole", with no reason given. The current all-or-nothing protects nothing for the xattr kind. A failed read stores an empty extended_attributes list, and an in-place restore (restore.rs:1722 -> haiku::set_xattrs -> apply with an empty want) then removes all of the file's B_XATTR_TYPE attributes. With the fix, only the unreadable one would be removed. Nuances for the fixer and the user: - For haiku.attributes, "consistency with the other backends" holds only partly. Both forks also keep FreeBSD/NetBSD system extattrs all-or-nothing (freebsd_netbsd.rs:309-315; restic-bko attrs_bsd.go:183-189). A partial map would make an in-place restore remove the attribute that couldn't be read. That is the same trade-off restic-bko already accepts for xattrs, and it is the user's call. - The restore-side stats() failure is rare on BFS, because listing has already loaded each attribute inode. - BACKOTTER.md:705 must change along with the fix.

column3: crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/illumos.rs:595-606 (restore_acls returns early when the node has no illumos.acl)
column4: Checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); module doc's own motivation (illumos.rs:4-6: 'access the ACL denied can come back allowed')
column6: A node without illumos.acl, meaning its ACL was trivial at backup, leaves the restored file's existing ACL as it is. Only chmod can make that ACL trivial again, and on a dataset with aclmode=passthrough chmod keeps named-user and named-group ACEs. So an in-place (or --exact) restore keeps access that the backed-up file didn't grant.
column7: On a ZFS dataset with aclmode=passthrough, common on SMB shares, /data/f had a trivial ACL when it was backed up. Afterwards someone adds `user:bob:read_data:allow`. `rustic restore --exact` (or a plain restore over the tree) restores f. The node has no illumos.acl, so restore_acls does nothing. chmod keeps bob's ACE under passthrough, and --exact may not even chmod a file whose node metadata matches. Bob keeps read access that the snapshot doesn't give him. With aclmode=restricted, chmod fails instead. The BSD backend (freebsd_netbsd::restore_acls) returns early the same way, and so does restic-bko's nodeRestoreACLs. From reading the code and ZFS aclmode semantics; not run.
column8: When a node is a regular file or directory from a BackOtter snapshot made on illumos (known_bko, plus an illumos-origin marker such as illumos.system_attributes being present), and it has no illumos.acl, reset a non-trivial ACL on the file to the trivial one for its mode. That is what acl_strip(3SEC) does: ACE_SETACL with owner@, group@ and everyone@ built from the mode. Do it only when get_ace shows the ACL isn't trivial. Leave nodes from other systems alone. Test on the guest: add a named ACE after the backup, restore in place, and check is_trivial(get_ace(f)). This is a behaviour change (D3), and F4 should judge the BSD twin.
column9: upgraded (S2->S1): I could not refute it. A run on OmniOS reproduces it, and by RA5's scale it is S1, not S2. **The code is ours.** illumos.rs was added by fcac5fa, a backotter: commit. git blame -w -M -C gives lines 592-606 to fcac5fa and 2c52ef2, both backotter: commits. **What the code does (ead8a63):** - `fill_acl` (illumos.rs:283) stores no `illumos.acl` for a trivial ACL. - `restore_acls` (illumos.rs:595-606) returns early without one, so nothing ever resets an ACL. Only `set_permission` does: a plain `chmod` (local_destination.rs:576-579), called from restore.rs:1735. - A plain restore runs `set_metadata` for every node in the stream (restore.rs:496, 1331). An identical file is left in place, same inode (restore.rs:822-830). - The finding's aside that "--exact may not even chmod" is wrong, but it doesn't help refute. In a BackOtter snapshot (`known_bko`), `exact::same_generic_attributes` (exact.rs:482-491) counts the file's extra `illumos.acl` as a mismatch. So `--exact` does chmod, cannot fix the ACL, and never converges: every run sets the metadata again and moves the ctime. **The run.** cinqcent, picked by pick-host, under `cmp-run.sh --reserve 1 5`, in a throwaway `--ram` omnios58 (OmniOS r151058y). The binary was rel11's illumos rustic-bko (rustic_core a04257f). a04257f..ead8a63 touches only the BSD extattr code and test formatting, nothing on this path. Files at backup were 0600, 0640 and 0644 files and a 0700 dir, all with trivial ACLs, and their nodes held only `unix.birthtime`. After the backup, `user:bob` ACEs were added. Then I ran a plain in-place restore, `--exact` and a fresh restore. - **aclmode=discard** (rpool: "discard default"): chmod resets the ACLs, so the result is correct. The failure needs a non-default aclmode. - **passthrough**: plain and `--exact` both exit 0 with no warning. bob still reads the 0600 root file and the 0640 file (he isn't in its group) and lists the 0700 dir. A deny ACE stays on the 0644 file, so bob loses access the snapshot gave him. - **groupmask**: bob's ACEs are masked to the group bits. He still reads the 0640 file, and the deny stays. Silent. - **restricted**: a "restore X: chmod failed." warning per file, exit 0, and bob keeps everything. - **Fresh restore**: correct. **Rules.** None of "Our rules that win" beats it: - Rule 3: the fix fits in our files and our own call line in restore.rs. - Rule 4: nodes and repository are unchanged and cross-restore still works. restic-bko's `nodeRestoreACLs` (attrs_illumos.go:314) has the same early return, so it should get the same fix (a courtesy, out of scope). - Rule 5: this is a behaviour change, so it goes to the user under D3. **Why S1.** RA5 puts "wrong result on real input, a privacy leak" in S1. Here a 0600 file stays readable by another user after a restore that exits 0 with no warning. The ledger already uses S1 for config-dependent wrong results (H9-05 on 4Kn disks, H6-02 on ZFS names). The finding's own rule cites S1's wording. **The fix sketch's marker doesn't work.** `illumos.system_attributes` is missing on most ZFS files: `kept_mask` (illumos_sysattr.rs:152-159) drops it when the mask equals archive+av_modified. The fixer needs another way to tell an illumos node, which is a D3 question. Output kept on the Mac: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-mchobbit-git-backotter/fbac8b1f-8f61-4216-bf95-431973e8cc08/scratchpad/f10-f504/result.txt. The host scratch dir is removed and the guest is gone.

column4: Checklist 2 and 8 (parsers refuse malformed input; F2 acl_and_sids_malformed)
column6: split_sid checks that the whole SID starts with "S-", not that the prefix does, so "S-1" splits as ("S", 1) and "S--1" as ("S-", 1). id_of_sid then hands libidmap a bogus prefix from the snapshot instead of refusing it as 'malformed SID'. This is F2's (c) defect.
column7: A snapshot holds illumos.owner_sid "S-1". restore_owner calls id_of_sid, which calls idmap_get_uidbysid(prefix "S", rid 1). idmapd either fails, so the file goes to nobody with an idmap status error instead of a 'malformed SID' one, or hands out an ephemeral id for the junk SID. F2's acl_and_sids_malformed test records 'cut "S-1": split as ("S", 1)' and fails until this is fixed.
column8: Require prefix.starts_with("S-") and at least one more '-' in the prefix, with a digit after "S-". Add "S-1" and "S--1" to split_sids' malformed list; F2's malformed-input test then passes.

column4: Checklist 1/5 (FFI hygiene: std opens every descriptor close-on-exec)
column6: attr_names duplicates the attribute directory with plain dup(2), and attr_dir_unopened takes __openattrdirat's descriptor, which is opened without O_CLOEXEC. Neither descriptor is close-on-exec, unlike every other open in the unit, where std or an explicit O_CLOEXEC sets it. A child process started by another thread meanwhile inherits them.
column7: While a backup thread is in attr_names, another thread spawns a process (a hook, or the ssh/rclone backend launched by std::process::Command). The child inherits an open descriptor for the file's attribute directory, and keeps it for as long as it runs. That holds the directory open and leaks access to it into the child.
column8: Use libc::fcntl(fd, F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC, 0) in place of dup. After __openattrdirat, set FD_CLOEXEC with fcntl(F_SETFD), or open the attribute directory with openat(AT_FDCWD, path, O_XATTR|O_CLOEXEC|O_RDONLY) where the file can be opened.

column4: Checklist 7 (doc against code) and 2
column6: attr_dir opens the base file to reach its attribute directory, which fails with EACCES for a file illumos quarantined. So a quarantined file's extended attributes and their metadata are never kept, and mapper.rs says they can't be read. sysattr_view in the same file reaches a quarantined file's attribute directory with __openattrdirat (illumos.rs:203-206, 220-222), and the attribute files themselves aren't quarantined.
column7: A vscan service sets av_quarantined on a non-empty file that has named attributes. The backup keeps the node without its contents, as designed, and also without its attributes or illumos.xattr_meta. A restore then brings the file back with no attributes, even though they were readable through __openattrdirat. restic-bko does the same (attrDir in xattr_illumos.go), so a change would go into both forks, or neither.
column8: Either have attr_dir fall back to attr_dir_unopened on EACCES for a regular file, as sysattr_view does, and drop the 'nor its extended attributes' clause in mapper.rs, in both forks. Or keep the behaviour and correct the comment to say they are left out by choice. Test on the guest: chmod S+vav_quarantined a file with an attribute, back it up, and its xattrs are there.

column4: Checklist 3 (errors say what failed)
column6: When attr_dir gives None because the node isn't a regular file or directory (a symlink, FIFO or device), set_xattrs reports each attribute as 'no extended attributes on this file system', which names the wrong cause.
column7: A Fedora snapshot restored onto illumos: every symlink there has security.selinux. Each one gives 'security.selinux: no extended attributes on this file system' on a ZFS dataset that does have them. The real reason is that illumos keeps no attributes on symlinks.
column8: Have attr_dir say why it gave None, or check the type in set_xattrs, and use 'no extended attributes are kept for this type of file' for those, as haiku.rs:227-230 does. This changes a warning's text, so it goes to the user (rule 5).

column6: The directory half of the R4-01 test checks that dir/x doesn't exist. But '..' in sub's attribute directory is sub itself, so an unrefused '../x' would create sub/x, and that path is never checked.
column7: Suppose a regression lets '../x' through for directories and the open happens to fail for another reason. Then dir/x stays absent and the exists() assert passes, while the escape went to sub/x. Today the is_err() assert catches the plain regression, but the exists() check guards the wrong path.
column8: Assert !sub.join("x").exists() as well, or in its place, and also that dir.path().join("x") is still absent.

column4: Checklist 2 (unwrap only on proven invariants, with the proof in the message); Book ch. 9
column6: be32 and be64 slice buf[pos..pos+N], which panics if the bytes aren't there, and then call try_into().unwrap() with no message. Every caller in parse, mask and crtime checks the length first, and F2's bit-flip run found no panic. But the precondition isn't written down, so a new caller can make the view decoder panic on bytes from disk.
column7: No panic is reachable today. If a future caller uses be32 on Pair.value without the has_boolean or len checks, a 2-byte boolean in a crafted or damaged view makes the backup thread panic.
column8: Have them return Option, using buf.get(pos..pos + 4) and u32::from_be_bytes, and use `?` at the call sites. Or document the precondition and use expect with the reason ('N bytes checked by the caller').

column3: crates/core/src/commands/restore.rs:496 (restore_metadata over every node after restore_contents at 485); files_writer.rs:289-296 (finish returns only a count); restore.rs:1760 (set_times)
column4: Checklist 3 (errors: no lost error, a partial restore must not look complete) and the bar's 'wrong result on real input'; Our rule 4 (stock rustic stops before metadata here)
column6: A file whose contents failed partway still gets its node's mtime in the metadata pass, so a plain re-run trusts its size and mtime and keeps the corrupt contents without a word.
column7: Plain restore, no --verify-existing. A 1 GiB file is sized at its first write (set_length does set_len to the full size), then a later write_at fails with EDQUOT or ENOSPC (set_length's preallocate is best effort). FilesWriter::fail reports it and the restore goes on. restore_metadata then calls set_metadata on every node, so set_times gives this file the snapshot's mtime. The restore ends with 'The contents of 1 files could not be restored' (exit 1). The user frees space and re-runs the same restore, as BACKOTTER.md advises for errors. match_file finds the right size and mtime and returns FileMatch::Existing, so the file counts as 'unchanged' and the run exits 0. Everything after the failed offset is still zeros or old data. The same happens on the skip path: a file that took one blob from a pack and lost another because its from_file source could not be read (test_restore_existing_file_gone_is_no_panic's set-up, with g sharing only part of f's chunks). It also happens to an existing same-size file whose open fails (ETXTBSY on a running binary): it keeps its old contents but gets the new mtime. Stock rustic panicked at the first failed write, before the metadata pass, so no mtime was ever set; this is a regression from our keep-going change.
column8: Have FilesWriter::finish return the failed file indices, map them to their snapshot paths (RestorePlan.names) and pass the set to restore_metadata. For those files skip set_times, or set an mtime no node can have, so that a re-run sees a mismatch and rewrites the file; keep the error count as it is. Test: an integration test that copies test_restore_existing_file_gone_is_no_panic but gives g only part of f's chunks plus its own. Replace f with a directory between the plan and the restore, expect the error, remove the directory, re-run with default options, and assert g's contents equal the snapshot's. It fails today.
column9: confirmed (S1->S1): I could not refute it. The code and two runs on the farm both confirm it. **Code (rustic_core ead8a63).** - `restore_repository` (restore.rs:485-516) always runs `restore_metadata` after `restore_contents`, whatever failed. `FilesWriter::finish` (files_writer.rs:289-296) returns only `failed.len()`. - `restore_metadata` calls `set_metadata` on every node except the unbroken ones and the hard-link names. `set_metadata` ends with `dest.set_times` (restore.rs:1760). - `set_length` (local_destination.rs:719) calls `set_len` to the full size at a file's first write. `preallocate` errors only reach the debug log, and on btrfs (non-NOCOW) and bcachefs it is never tried. - `match_file` (restore.rs:2653) returns `Existing` when size and mtime match, unless `--verify-existing`. That check is upstream's, but the regression comes from our keep-going change. - The lines are ours. `git blame -w -M -C` gives restore.rs:485 and 506-515 to ccc68a28, 496 to b4337fa4 and 497-503 to 1a2a4a47/b660a71e, all `backotter:` commits. files_writer.rs is a file we added. **Runs.** I used the debug build rustic 0.11.4+backotter.22 (3853eb3 + ead8a63) from cinqcent's bko-audit fork directory. It ran under `cmp-run.sh --reserve 1 1` with `WEAR_TAG audit:forkaudit1-f10-f601`, in /mnt/bko-ram, which I have since removed. 1. **ENOSPC.** The target was a 16 MiB tmpfs (in `unshare -rm`) holding an 11 MiB filler file, and the snapshot had a 6 MiB, a 2 MiB and a 6-byte file. - Run 1 exited 1 with "restore big: contents not restored ... No space left on device". `big` was left at the full 6291456 bytes with the snapshot's mtime (2020-01-02 03:04:05.123456789), and its contents differed from byte 3141633 on. - I removed the filler and re-ran the same plain restore. It exited 0, printing "Files: 0 to restore, 2 unchanged, 0 verified, 1 to modify" (the `fill_holes` pass), "all file contents are fine." and "restore done." `big` still differed. - Only a third run with `--verify-existing` repaired it. 2. **EACCES.** As non-root, I restored over an existing read-only (0444) file `z` of the snapshot's size, filled with zeros. - Run A exited 1 with "opening file failed: Permission denied". `z` kept its zeros but got mode 644 and the snapshot's mtime. - Run B exited 0 with "0 to restore, 3 unchanged ... all file contents are fine." `z` still held zeros. 3. **Stock rustic 0.11.4, same ENOSPC set-up.** It panicked at rustic_core-0.13.0 restore.rs:663 (`write_at(...).unwrap()`) with exit 101 and never reached the metadata pass, so the mtimes were the write times. The plain re-run then reported "2 verified, 1 to modify" and `big` came out equal to the snapshot. So this is a regression from our keep-going change. **Rules.** None beats the finding. - Rule 3: the fix fits in our own hunks of restore.rs plus files_writer.rs. - Rule 4: node parity and cross-restore are untouched. restic-bko also gives failed files their metadata (`fileList` keeps them, and `restoreNodeMetadataTo` runs in the second pass). But its default `--overwrite always` verifies blob by blob, so its plain re-run repairs the file. - Rule 5: the fix changes restored attributes and output, so it goes to the user (`changes_output` true). **Severity.** S1 stands: real input (a target that fills, or a read-only file in the way) leads to a re-run that reports success and exits 0 over wrong contents. bko-holt's main restore is a plain `restore --numeric-id`, so re-running its restore stage on the same target hits this. **Small inaccuracies in the finding.** - With a BackOtter snapshot, the corrupt file can count as "to modify" (`fill_holes`) rather than "unchanged". It still exits 0. - BACKOTTER.md does not explicitly advise re-running after content errors. - The proposed `from_file` test may pass today rather than fail. - The `from_file` reads come first, and a directory fails at once, so `g` can fail before any write sizes it; it is then never created and gets restored whole. - `PackInfo::coalesce` also merges a `from_file` blob into a pack read that comes just before it in the same pack. - Deterministic tests: the non-root read-only same-size file, or a small tmpfs with root or a user namespace.

column4: Checklist 3 (errors carry what failed), API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR
column6: set_metadata has the error in hand and counts it, but its warnings for chown, chmod and file times print only 'setting X failed.' without the error; neighbouring warnings in the same function (create_special, extended attributes, symlink mode, birth time) include it.
column7: Run as root, restoring a stock rustic snapshot (origin Other, so node_sets_flags is false and flags stay) over an existing immutable file. chmod and utimensat fail with EPERM. The log says only 'restore f: chmod failed.' and 'restore f: setting file times failed.'. LocalDestination::error_counts counts both (root, EPERM), so --strict-exit fails with 'There were 2 errors', and nothing tells the user that EPERM, the immutable flag, EROFS or EDQUOT was the cause. The LocalDestination setters don't log the error themselves.
column8: warn!("restore {}: setting {what} failed: {err}"), and the same ': {err}' for chmod and set_times. These lines are already ours (blamed to backotter: commits), so rule 3 allows it. Test: a unit test with a captured logger, or an integration test as root that chattr +i's an existing file before a stock-origin restore and checks the warning contains 'Operation not permitted'.
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): F6-02 stands. I could not refute it from the code, and a run on a host reproduced it. The code, at rustic_core ead8a63: - In crates/core/src/commands/restore.rs, three warnings in set_metadata have `err` in hand but leave it out of the text: 1700 (`setting {what} failed.` for UID/GID and User/Group), 1741 (`chmod failed.`) and 1761 (`setting file times failed.`). - RestoreTally::dest (437-441) only counts; it logs nothing. - The LocalDestination setters (set_times 348, set_user_group 407, set_uid_gid 460, set_permission 558) only map_err and return. - No other place reports these errors. rustic 3853eb3 then bails with "There were N errors (see the warnings above)" (src/commands/restore.rs:196). The warnings it points to give no cause. - The other warnings in the same function do give the cause: create_special `: {err}`, extended attributes `: {err}`, symlink mode and birth time `{err}`, and tally.io through osattrs::warn_restore. - The doc of node_sets_flags (osattrs.rs:412-416) says that where a file's flags refuse the restore, "its error says so". For these three steps it doesn't. The host run, on Cinqcent (kernel 7.2.12, tmpfs, under cmp-run.sh --reserve 1 1, WEAR_TAG audit:f10:F6-02; the scratch dir was removed afterwards): - Stock rustic 0.11.4 (bko-audit/stock) backed up a small tree. - rustic-bko 0.11.4+backotter.22, built at exactly 3853eb3+ead8a63 (bko-audit/fork/rustic-3853eb3c274b+core-ead8a632a500), restored it as root. I then ran chattr +i on the restored f and restored again. - With the default owners (by name), the log said only "restore f: setting User/Group failed.", "restore f: chmod failed." and "restore f: setting file times failed.", then "error: There were 3 errors", exit 1. - With --no-ownership it gave exactly the finding's case: the chmod and file-times warnings, then "There were 2 errors". Nothing in either run named EPERM. - The stated failure case is therefore slightly understated. By default, chown also fails on an immutable file (Linux may_setattr), so there are three warnings without a cause. Whether the line is upstream's: - The text is upstream's word for word. Both 1030be4 (the 0.13.0 base) and upstream/main d658ed9 still discard the error with `|_|`. - But `git blame -w -M -C` gives all three lines to backotter: commits 9387171 and b4337fa, and `git diff 1030be4 ead8a63` shows them as + lines. column4: 1 Soundness (no TOCTOU on paths a privileged process trusts); 7 Docs (doc against code)
column6: The links' directory is checked only when it is made (mkdir 0700). After that, every link is made and followed by its path, $TMPDIR/.bko-longpath-PID-N/k, which is never checked again. If any component of the canonical $TMPDIR sits in a directory another user can write to (not sticky, or owned by that user), that user can rename the directory away and put their own in its place, with symlinks named 0..n. A root restore then makes, chowns, chmods and writes files through those symlinks, wherever the other user points them.
column7: Root runs `rustic-bko restore` with TMPDIR=/home/bob/tmp (inherited by `sudo -E` or `su` without `-`, or a shared scratch TMPDIR of mode 0777 without the sticky bit), over a snapshot with paths past PATH_MAX. bob, who owns /home/bob, renames tmp/.bko-longpath-PID-0 within its own parent, which needs no write permission on the root-owned directory. He makes a new .bko-longpath-PID-0 whose '0' -> /home/bob/trap, where trap/<next names of the restore path> lead by symlink into /etc. root's next create_dir, set_length or set_user_group on a long item resolves L_0/rest through bob's link: root creates directories and files with snapshot-chosen names in an attacker-chosen directory and chowns them to the snapshot's uid (fchownat's NOFOLLOW covers only the last component). The doc claim that it is 'a new one only this process can enter' holds for the directory's contents, not for its name. With TMPDIR unset (/tmp, root-owned and sticky) this can't happen, so it needs that environment.
column8: In make_dir, before making the directory, walk the canonical tmp's components and refuse (an io::Error saying which component and why, which then reaches report_short_path_errors) any component that is not owned by root or the euid, or that is group- or other-writable without the sticky bit, as OpenSSH's safe_path does. Optionally, also record the links directory's (dev, ino) and lstat-check it under LINKS before making each new link. Document the trust assumption in the module doc and in BACKOTTER.md. Test: a child-process test (the existing `child` helper) with TMPDIR under a 0777 non-sticky directory asserts that try_short_path errs and names that directory. Output changes only in that environment: a new warning, and long paths fail as ENAMETOOLONG there.
column9: downgraded (S2->S3): The code is ours: vendor/walkdir/src/longpath.rs is a file we added, so neither rule 3 nor any other rule beats the finding. The mechanism is real. make_dir (lines 315-338) checks the links' directory only by its mkdir 0700. link_to (line 282) and every short path after that go through $TMPDIR/.bko-longpath-PID-N/k by name, so someone who can rename an entry in the canonical tmp could swap the directory. But the failure case as written cannot happen through the routes it names. On Chopin, `TMPDIR=/home/m/xtmp sudo -n -E sh -c 'echo $TMPDIR'` printed an empty value, even with --preserve-env=TMPDIR. FOO=bar did come through. glibc's secure mode (AT_SECURE, UNSECURE_ENVVARS) strips TMPDIR from setuid programs, and su is setuid too, so neither `sudo -E` nor `su` without `-` passes an untrusted TMPDIR to root on glibc. On musl (Alpine, Void musl, Chimera), su without `-` would keep TMPDIR, but it also hands root bob's PATH, LD_PRELOAD and ENV, so bob already controls root's process and no new boundary is crossed. The only case left is root, or root's admin, choosing on purpose a TMPDIR that another user owns or can write to without the sticky bit. That breaks the usual rule that TMPDIR is trusted, and it breaks every mktemp/mkstemp user the same way (files reopened by path can be renamed and replaced). glibc and POSIX don't check this, and BackOtter never does it: rustic-bko runs with /tmp on the rescue stick, and holt sets TMPDIR only for mktemp inside a chroot (commands.rs:5564). What remains is a hardening idea and a doc wording issue. "A new one only this process can enter" (doc lines 311-314) and BACKOTTER.md's "a new one only it made" are true of the directory's contents, not of its name in a writable parent. So: S3, a docs note stating that $TMPDIR and its parents are trusted to be root's (or the euid's) or sticky. The safe_path check is optional hardening that would change output, and it is not owed as a soundness fix.

It is reachable through library callers without with_parents, and in the error case above.

column6: 3027d2b is ours: author MC Hobbit, unpushed, and only formatting and a closure rename, as rustic BACKOTTER.md:337-340 says ('behaves as .21'). Its subject lacks 'backotter:', so rust-scope.sh counts its lines as upstream.
column7: Today nothing is lost, because its 4 files were added whole by backotter: commits. But a rebase script or a scope run that filters on the prefix treats it as upstream. If a later unprefixed commit touches an upstream file, blame-based scope silently drops those lines from the audit.
column8: Reword the subject to 'backotter: ...' before the branch is pushed (it is local). This rewrites unpushed history, so it is the user's call. Alternatively, make rust-scope.sh also count the fork author's commits without the prefix and flag them.

column6: 'Building' step 1 says to run `cargo update -p rustic_core -p walkdir` after rustic_core's branch moves. The last two lock commits (9ddbbaf, 3853eb3) record a different procedure: `cargo update -p rustic_core --precise <sha>`, because the fork commits are unpushed and the branch dependency resolves to GitHub's tip. They also hand-revert the windows-sys and getrandom re-resolution that this causes.
column7: Following the doc while rustic_core's commits are unpushed pins GitHub's older branch tip. build-backotter.sh's bko_core check then stops the build, with a message telling you to push, which the audit rules forbid. A pushed run also re-resolves windows-sys and getrandom, which the commits say they leave out.

It is c_long (32-bit) on gnu b32 mips and riscv32. - gnu/b64/mod.rs:23 also makes it i32 on x32, so x86_64-unknown-linux-gnux32 is affected too. - musl/mod.rs:353 has f_type as c_ulong; 64-bit gnu has i64 (b64/mod.rs:25). Both are positive, so try_from succeeds there. - linux_like/mod.rs:1944-1947 links statfs/fstatfs to the 64-bit symbols only under gnu_file_offset_bits64, which the forks do not set. So the non-LFS calls, and their EOVERFLOW, are real on 32-bit glibc. - Debian glibc 2.41-12+deb13u4, /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/statfs.h:26 declares `__fsword_t f_type`, matching the binding. FAILURE CASE: on i686-gnu or armv7-gnueabihf, u32::try_from(negative i32) is Err, so is_on(f, BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC) and is_bcachefs_path are always false. file_projid then skips bcachefs_effective.project, and the restore's bcachefs branches are skipped. The ZFS, XFS and MSDOS magics are positive and unaffected. NO RULE WINS: no repository or node format change (rule 4). restic-bko does not share it. column7: On powerpc, mips and sparc Linux (admitted by cfg target_os = linux) _IOC_WRITE is 4 at shift 29, so FICLONE is 0x8004_9409: `restore --clone-from` sends an unknown ioctl, gets ENOTTY for every file and never clones (it falls back, so no data is wrong). x86_64 and aarch64 are right.
column8: `const FICLONE: libc::Ioctl = libc::_IOW::<libc::c_int>(0x94, 9);` and a test that `FICLONE as u32 == 0x4004_9409` on x86_64/aarch64 (as u32, so it also runs on musl, see R2-07).
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): Not refuted. Prior row R1-02 already carries a confirmed second-read verdict, and the cited code is unchanged in substance at rustic_core f0d01fd: crates/core/src/backend/osattrs.rs:321 is still `const FICLONE: libc::Ioctl = 0x4004_9409;` (was line 309), under `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` with no arch gate. - **Ours:** `git blame -w -M -C` gives lines 316-326 to e79e45a "backotter: 0.13.0+backotter.8: restore --exact and clone sources". - **Inconsistency holds:** osattrs/linux.rs:89-130 builds every ioctl number with `libc::_IOR`/`libc::_IOW`. - **Headers (Chopin, linux-libc-dev 7.2.12-1~bpo13+1):** /usr/include/linux/fs.h:315 is `#define FICLONE _IOW(0x94, 9, int)`. /usr/lib/linux/uapi/{powerpc,mips,sparc}/asm/ioctl.h each set `_IOC_SIZEBITS 13`, `_IOC_DIRBITS 3`, `_IOC_WRITE 4U`, so the direction shift is 29 and FICLONE is (4<<29)|(4<<16)|(0x94<<8)|9 = 0x8004_9409. asm-generic (x86, arm64) has SIZEBITS 14, DIRBITS 2, `_IOC_WRITE 1U`, giving 0x4004_9409. The literal is therefore right on x86_64/aarch64 and wrong on powerpc, mips and sparc Linux. - **Failure case is real but benign:** on those arches the ioctl is unknown and returns ENOTTY. clone_contents returns the errno to clone_over_with (exact.rs:193), and the prior second read traced that path to CloneFailed::Failed and the restore's fallback; I did not re-trace it past exact.rs:193. No data goes wrong and no shipped target (x86_64, aarch64) is affected. Not run on a powerpc/mips/sparc target; the header arithmetic settles it. - **No winning rule beats it:** the fix is one line in our own code (rule 3 is fine), with no repo-format or output change. - **Simpler fix than the finding sketches:** libc 0.2.191 (Cargo.lock at f0d01fd) defines `pub const FICLONE: Ioctl = _IOW::<c_int>(0x94, 9)` at src/unix/linux_like/mod.rs:1516, so `libc::FICLONE` can replace the local constant, subject to that definition's cfg gate, which I did not read (the earlier ledger note says it excludes only emscripten/l4re). The finding's `libc::_IOW::<libc::c_int>(0x94, 9)` is equally correct. Severity stays S2 to match the confirmed prior row. column6: New. The code and docs say FreeBSD has no ACLs on symlinks, so fill_acls and restore_acls skip them there. FreeBSD does have them: __acl_get_link/__acl_set_link work on a symlink (setfacl -h), and on UFS mounted acls a symlink made in a directory with a default ACL inherits an extended access ACL (releng/15.0 sys/ufs/ufs/ufs_vnops.c:2344 ufs_symlink -> ufs_makeinode -> 2897 ufs_do_posix1e_acl_inheritance_file, no VLNK exemption). column7: Live, FreeBSD 15.1-p6, rel13 rustic-bko at f0d01fd, UFS md mounted acls: `setfacl -d -m u::rwx,g::rx,o::rx,u:mallory:r,m::rx d; ln -s target d/link` gives link user:mallory:r-- and mask::r-x (ls shows lrwxr-xr-x+); `setfacl -h -m u:mallory:rw plainlink` works too (also on ZFS: user:mallory:r:allow on a symlink). After restore, getfacl -h shows only user/group/other on both, and plainlink comes back with group::rwx where the source had group::r-x under mask rwx (the mode's group bits, which held the mask, became the group's permission). Access through a symlink does not depend on its ACL, so this is lost metadata, not lost protection.

So already_matches fails, set_metadata runs, and nothing resets the flag. Each os::file_flags returns None for no flags (linux.rs:362-368; NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly filter 0; FreeBSD through freebsd_file_flags; illumos through kept_mask). The metadata pass is one sequential loop, so no interleaving is involved. DOCS: this is not an accepted limit, the docs promise the opposite. rustic_core BACKOTTER.md 561-562 says the late flag pass gives every file its node's flags, 774-780 says a BackOtter node's missing attribute was none and only other snapshots leave the destination as it is, 1279-1287 has the --exact text the finding quotes, and rustic BACKOTTER.md 220-226 says the same. After chflags nodump on a file, uarch on another, hidden on a directory, nodump on a symlink and on a hard-linked file, three runs of RUSTIC_STRICT_EXIT=true restore --numeric-id --exact each exited 0 with no warning; all five flags stayed and all five ctimes moved on every run (...524, ...526, ...528).
