With uchg,nodump on one file, --exact took uchg off and left nodump. A backup of the result records freebsd.file_flags 1 and 32768 where the snapshot's nodes have none. On ZFS, nodump on a file whose node has no attribute stayed (uarch,nodump) over three runs with the ctime moving each time, and the control whose node holds 0 converged. restic-bko rel13 on the same UFS behaves the same (nodump stays, ctime moves on each of three --exact runs, exit 0): restorer.go:444-463 queues only when hasFlags, and exact.go:461-483 counts the missing attribute. Linux 7.2.12, not root, tmpfs and XFS: chattr +d on a restored file whose node has no linux.inode_flags stayed over three --exact runs, ctime moving each run, and over a plain restore; a node that holds the flag converged. NEW, and it makes the case reachable without anyone setting a flag on the file: on Linux a file the restore creates in an existing directory that carries an inheritable flag gets that flag. Source: d has nodump, d/old was made before it and has none, so its node has no attribute. The fresh restore is right. After rm dst/d/old and a second restore, dst/d/old comes back with nodump on tmpfs and on XFS, and --exact then moves its ctime on every run. RULES: none wins. Rule 3: the fix sites are our lines and files. Rule 4: the fix is restore-side only, nodes and repository unchanged. Rule 5: it changes what a restore does to existing files, so it is changes-output, which the user approved fixing. SEVERITY: S2 stands. The result is wrong and silent, but these flags grant no access and lose no data, as with F5-02 (S2); its ACL twins F4-01 and F5-04 are S1 for the access they leave. CORRECTIONS AND NOTES FOR THE FIXERS (G3/G6): (a) On FreeBSD ZFS the uarch half heals itself: chflags nouarch on a file whose node has no attribute came back as uarch after one --exact run and then converged, because ZFS sets ZFS_ARCHIVE on any ctime change (FreeBSD 15.1 zfs_znode_os.c, zfs_tstamp_update_setup_ext, AT_CTIME). Other flags on ZFS do not heal. (b) The no-attribute value is not 0 everywhere: UF_ARCHIVE on FreeBSD ZFS as the finding says, and on illumos the automatic mask the file's view has (archive, av_modified; illumos_sysattr.rs:152-159). The same Option-only shape sits beside it for linux.zfs_dos_flags (archive alone, linux.rs:660-663) and linux.fat_attrs (linux.rs:420-424) at restore.rs:1334-1335. (c) Do not queue every entry: a plain restore sets every entry's metadata, so LatePass would hold a row per file. Read the file's flags and queue only where they differ from the no-attribute value. That also avoids two side effects of calling restore_file_flags with nothing to change: OpenBSD passes current as None (openbsd.rs:77), so on a file system without flags a value of 0 would give an Unsupported warning; FreeBSD, NetBSD and illumos call lchflags or write the view before comparing. (d) Linux FS_NOCOW_FL cannot be cleared late on a file with data (btrfs ignores it without an error, linux.rs:58-60): an inherited C has to come off when the file is created empty, as prepare_dir does for casefolding, or stay a documented limit. (e) The other-OS guard would be new behaviour: node_flags already answers Some(0) for any BackOtter node without this OS's attribute, and restricting flags are cleared on that basis today. Decide both halves together; a snapshot has no OS field. (f) restic-bko needs the same at restorer.go:444-463: queue the no-attribute value when the node has no flags and the snapshot is from BackOtter. Not changed here. column7: Live, FreeBSD 15.1-p6, rel13 rustic-bko at f0d01fd: a ZFS dataset holding a directory, a file, a symlink (all uarch), a file with archive cleared (`chflags nouarch`) and a file with `zfs project -p 42`. Backed up directly: no flags attribute on the three, freebsd.file_flags 0 on the cleared one, freebsd.zfs_project {"id":42}. Backed up through `mount -t nullfs`: freebsd.file_flags 2048 on every uarch entry, none on the cleared one (so a restore onto ZFS gives it archive back), and no freebsd.zfs_project at all: the project ID is lost without a warning, exit 0.
column8: Decide ZFS by what the file answers, not by the mount's name: once per device, open the entry (or its directory) and try ZFS_IOC_FSGETXATTR, which only ZFS implements (ENOTTY elsewhere); check on the guest that nullfs passes the ioctl through. Following f_mntfromname does not work inside a jail. restic-bko shares it (internal/fs/flags_freebsd.go:65, project_freebsd.go) and must change with it. It changes what a backup records under nullfs. Test: the nullfs case above gives the same nodes as the direct backup. [Changes output; fixing approved 2026-11-22.]
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): Not refuted: I reproduced the failure independently, and no rule beats it. The prior row F4-08 carried only "unread-s3", so this was a full second read. **Code (rustic_core f0d01fd).** `freebsd.rs` `on_zfs` (177-200) caches per `st_dev` whether `fs_type()` (203-212, `statfs(2)` `f_fstypename`) equals "zfs". Both backup-side callers depend on it: `file_flags` (168) and `open_for_attrs` (55, which returns `None` when not on ZFS, so `fill_zfs_project` never runs and nothing is logged). `bsd_flags.rs:26` `freebsd_file_flags(flags, zfs=false)` keeps 0x800 and drops 0. **Scope.** The lines are ours: blame gives 5b3e56c, 62af33f and d26df1a, all "backotter:" commits, in a file we added. **Live run.** cinqcent, throwaway freebsd15 guest via `guest-run.sh --ram`, FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE-p6, the rel13 binary `roundrel13/bin/freebsd/rustic-bko` (sha 31c06cb1..., rustic 0.12.0+backotter.1). A file-backed pool with dataset `g404pool/ds`, also mounted with `mount -t nullfs` on `/nt`: - **What the system reports:** `df -T` gives "zfs" for the dataset and "nullfs" for `/nt`. `st_dev` differs between the two. `st_flags` are identical through nullfs (0x800 on dir, file and symlink; 0 on the `chflags nouarch` file). - **Direct backup:** `cleared` has `freebsd.file_flags` 0; `d`, `f`, `l` have no flags attribute; `proj` has `freebsd.zfs_project {"id":42}`. - **Backup through nullfs:** `cleared` has no attribute; `d`, `f`, `l`, `proj` have `freebsd.file_flags` 2048; there is no `freebsd.zfs_project` anywhere. Exit 0, and nothing about it even at debug log level. - **Restore onto ZFS:** the nullfs snapshot gives `cleared` uarch back and `proj` project 0. The direct snapshot restores both correctly (no flag, project 42). **Rules.** Rule 3 does not apply (our file). Rule 4 does not block: the nodes stay readable, only rustic-bko's nodes under nullfs would differ from restic-bko's until restic-bko follows, and that parity is a courtesy. restic-bko has the same defect (`internal/fs/flags_freebsd.go` `isZFS`, same statfs test; `project_freebsd.go`) and is not to be changed here. Rule 5: it changes output, which the user approved on 2026-11-22. **Severity.** S2 stands. By the letter, "wrong result on real input" is S1. But it needs nullfs over ZFS (jails) plus a project ID or an archive-cleared file to lose anything, and contents and all other metadata are intact. **For the fixer.** - The proposed probe is workable: `zfs project` through `/nt` returned 42 with rc 0, so nullfs passes `ZFS_IOC_FSGETXATTR` to ZFS. - The probe needs an openable regular file or directory. For a symlink or special file, probe its directory; if it cannot be opened, fall back to statfs. - Check that the ioctl also succeeds on a pool without the `project_quota` feature. Otherwise ZFS there would be taken for non-ZFS. - Only the backup side uses `on_zfs`; the restore paths do not. Host scratch (`~/backotter-work/g404-sr`, `logs/guest-run-freebsd15-2967`) is removed and the guest is powered off.

column6: [restates R3-03] R3-03 stands. FreeBSD keeps its own copy of chmod_symlink through a hand-declared lchmod, with another error policy: every failure is a per-symlink error, where chmod_symlink (NetBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFly) sends EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL to the debug log. restic-bko's lchmod (internal/fs/symlinkmode_bsd.go:28) ignores those two on every BSD, so FreeBSD is also off parity here.
column7: A restore on FreeBSD onto a file system whose lchmod(2) answers EOPNOTSUPP or EINVAL reports one error per restored symlink and, with strict exit, a failing exit status; rustic-bko on the other BSDs and restic-bko on FreeBSD report none. Which FreeBSD file systems answer so is still not checked on a guest.
column8: Add target_os = "freebsd" to chmod_symlink's cfg (FreeBSD has fchmodat with AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW; releng/15.0 sys/sys/stat.h declares lchmod at 385), make freebsd::restore_symlink_mode call it, delete the extern block. [Changes output; fixing approved 2026-11-22.]
column9: confirmed (S2->S2): Confirmed quickly: prior row R3-03 (findings.tsv line 225) already carries a confirmed second read, and the cited code is unchanged in substance at rustic_core f0d01fd. - **Code still as cited.** `crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/freebsd.rs:46-48` hand-declares `lchmod`, and 291-301 `restore_symlink_mode` turns every failure into `path_error("lchmod", ...)`. `osattrs.rs:1687` still leaves `freebsd` out of `chmod_symlink`'s cfg (dragonfly, netbsd, openbsd only), and that function sends EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL to the debug log. NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly all call the shared function. - **Ours.** `git blame -w -M -C` gives all cited lines to 62af33f and 1b9abcb0, both "backotter:" commits. - **No winning rule beats it.** The fix stays in our own files (rule 3), touches no repository format (rule 4), and sets the mode wherever the file system keeps one, so restore fidelity is not traded away. Rule 5 only makes it a user decision, which the user gave on 2026-11-22 ("Fix them"). - **restic-bko parity claim is right.** `internal/fs/symlinkmode_bsd.go:26-37` uses `Fchmodat(AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW)` on all four BSDs and ignores EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL, so restic-bko needs no change. One correction to the failure text, the same one the first second read made: the "failing exit status" holds only for EINVAL. - The caller is now `commands/restore.rs:1745`, which warns and calls `tally.count(&err, true)`. - `path_error` keeps the error kind, and std maps EOPNOTSUPP to `ErrorKind::Unsupported` (std `sys/io/error/unix.rs:185`, read on cinqcent's nightly-2026-10-31 rust-src). `restore_error_counts` (`osattrs.rs:1097`) does not count that kind. - So EOPNOTSUPP on FreeBSD gives one warning line per symlink but no counted error and no failing exit. EINVAL (InvalidInput) is counted and would fail a strict exit. Not run on a guest: which FreeBSD file systems answer EOPNOTSUPP or EINVAL to `lchmod` is still unchecked. I could not rule the case out, and the duplicated logic with a second error policy is S2 under checklist 6 and 3 on its own. The fix changes output: on FreeBSD the per-symlink warning for those two errnos becomes a debug line, and EINVAL is no longer counted.

Nothing checks that a cached link still exists.
column7: Reproduced on Chopin with rel13's rustic-bko 0.12.0+backotter.1. Source: `aaa/<120 x 40-byte dirs>/leaf` (4.9 KB) and `tmp/keep`. Restore once to dst, unlink the deep leaf in dst, then `TMPDIR=dst/tmp rustic-bko restore --delete latest:src dst`. Output: 'Files: 1 to restore ... Dirs: 0 to restore, 122 to modify, 1 additional', 'restore done.', exit 0. The leaf is missing afterwards and its directory is empty; dst/tmp holds only `keep`. The same command with TMPDIR outside dst restores the leaf. Needs a snapshot path of PATH_MAX bytes or more that sorts before $TMPDIR under the destination, so the links exist when the walk lists $TMPDIR. Typical setups: an in-place `restore --delete /` on a system with /tmp on disk, or TMPDIR under $HOME when restoring $HOME. The rescue-stick flow (target under /mnt, TMPDIR=/tmp) is not affected. A snapshot node of another type at $TMPDIR's path removes the directory the same way without --delete.

column6: The rel13 blocker. Root cause found and reproduced on Cinqcent; it is not a race inside one run. The test expects its three backups of one file to give the same tree. In the fork a snapshot of a path saved under its own name holds the directories above it with their own times (66d95b2), and one of those is the shared TMPDIR, whose mtime moves as other tests make and remove their directories. When the tree changes between the first and second backup but not between the second and third, the second backup writes a tree pack T2, and two upstream defects then meet. (1) prune_repository writes a stale plan's new index before it finds the plan's old index files gone: the test's stale plan2 leaves an index that lists T2 unmarked, and marks for recovery two packs that no longer exist, beside the newer index in which plan3 marked T2 for deletion. The third backup trusts the unmarked entry and does not store its root tree again. (2) repair_index keeps a pack's entry from whichever index file it reads first, whatever its mark. When it reads the delete-marked entry first, T2 stays marked for deletion only, and check reports the third snapshot's tree as not found in the index. Stock never writes a T2 in this test, because it gives the directories above a path nodes of its own making; G2 showed stock fails the same way (36 of 60) once the backed-up file itself changes. No hunk of ours is in prune, check, repair or the index, and the state is no data loss: T2 still exists and the next prune would recover it.

column6: New in the ledger; G2 measured it and the rebase did not change it. A node time is written at the system zone's offset for that instant. Where that offset has seconds (the zone's local mean time, before it took a standard time), RFC 3339 has no place for them: our function passes the offset on, the string keeps the local time with the offset cut to minutes, and the time reads back wrong by those seconds. Our function already writes UTC as `Z`; it should do the same for an offset RFC 3339 can't hold. The else branch is upstream's expression moved into our function, so stock rustic has the same defect.
column7: Measured by G2 on Cinqcent with TZ=Europe/Paris: a file with mtime 1850-06-01 12:00:00 UTC is stored as "1850-06-01T12:09:21+00:09" and every restore gives 12:00:21, 21 s late, in all four directions (restic-bko writes the same string). By the tz database, and not run: with TZ=Africa/Monrovia, whose offset was -0:44:30 until 1972-01-07, any file dated 1970 or 1971 is hit, epoch-dated files such as a Nix store's (mtime 1) among them.
column8: In timestamp_to_string write `ts.to_string()` (UTC, `Z`) also when `offset.seconds() % 60 != 0`; add both cases to node_times_as_restic_writes_them (the Paris one above, and a round trip through the parser). Only nodes with such times get different tree bytes; every reader takes `Z`, so rule 4 holds. Times already stored stay as they are. restic-bko shares it and is not to be changed here: it would need to write a node time in UTC when its zone offset is not a whole number of minutes. Until then the two tools' nodes differ for such files by those seconds, with rustic-bko's the right one. [Changes output; fixing approved 2026-11-22.]

Z for UTC node times". The offset on :136 is upstream's, and stock 0.14.0 has the same expression inline, so the defect is inherited. R7-02 is the precedent: an inherited defect on a line blame gives us was confirmed, not closed as upstream. - **Failure is real:** jiff 0.2.46 (source read on Chopin) prints the local time using the full offset, then prints the offset rounded to the nearest minute. So 12:00:00 UTC at +00:09:21 becomes "12:09:21+00:09" and reads back as 12:00:21, which matches what G2 measured. - **Zones confirmed on Chopin with date(1):** Europe/Paris is +00:09:21 in 1850 and still at 1901-12-13 (INT32_MIN, a common garbage mtime). Asia/Kolkata is +05:21:10 at that same instant. Africa/Monrovia is -00:44:30 at epoch 1. - **No bko guard:** nothing in the backotter repo sets TZ for a backup, so the source machine's zone applies. - **Rules:** none of "Our rules that win" beats it. The fix stays inside our own function (rule 3). Every reader takes `Z` (rule 4). The user's restore-fidelity rule supports the finding. - **Fix as proposed is sound:** writing `ts.to_string()` when `offset.seconds() % 60 != 0` changes tree bytes only for such nodes. Two corrections to the finding's wording: - jiff rounds the offset (30 s or more goes up); it does not cut it. For Paris the string is the same either way. - For Monrovia, rustic-bko would write "-00:45" and read back 30 s late. Go truncates, so restic-bko would write "-00:44" and read back 30 s early. The two tools already differ there by 60 s. This is from reading jiff and recalling Go's formatter, not run. After the fix, rustic-bko's node differs from restic-bko's for these times until restic-bko writes UTC for such offsets. Cross-restore still works. Severity stays S2: the result is silently wrong on legitimate input, but the error is under a minute and needs both a non-UTC zone and a date before that zone's whole-minute standard time (1970-71 in Liberia only).

column3: ~/git/rustic_core e54794d (G3-01), crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/linux.rs restore_flags_with -> set_all_late; crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/errors.rs warn_restore
column4: review of unit G3's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: New cosmetic miscount on the fallback path. Where FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR is missing or sets the wrong bits (OpenZFS 2.2, old kernels), a node with btrfs.compression plus i or a, restored onto a file system that refuses a flag such as FS_COMPR_FL, now yields two Unsupported errors of the same kind for one file: one from the first FS_IOC_SETFLAGS, one from set_all_late's. warn_restore adds 1 to that kind for each, so report_unsupported's summary says "linux.inode_flags 0x4 not supported by the file system: 2N files" for N files. Before the fix .and() kept only the first. The warning text, the exit code and the restored flags are right; only the number is doubled. Not covered by a test: restore_flags_compression_on_zfs_xflags's mock `set` never refuses. Fix idea: drop a later error whose Unsupported kind equals an earlier one in the same RestoreErrors, or count per file in warn_restore.

column4: review of unit G3's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: G3-01's symptom (a) is only half gone for the user. The flags path no longer warns "set btrfs.compression of F" on ext4/XFS/ZFS, but the xattr pass still warns once per file "setting extended attributes failed: btrfs.compression: Operation not supported" (not counted), where restic-bko says nothing according to the fixer (stock handleXattrErr drops ENOTSUP). The fixer reported this itself as outside G3; I found no ledger row for it (grep of findings.tsv). It belongs to unit G7's file. restic needs nothing.

column4: review of unit G3's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: One statfs reader was left on plain libc::fstatfs / libc::statfs for Linux and Android while the commit moved the magic readers to fstatfs64 because the plain call can fail with EOVERFLOW on 32-bit glibc. There fs_block_size returns None and hole_block_size falls back to st_blksize. Only 32-bit glibc builds, none shipped; no wrong data.

column3: proof of efe75bf and 8da87b4 (G3-02, G3-03): crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/sparse/seek.rs mod lfs, the target_env = "musl" arm
column4: review of unit G3's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: Proof gap, not a defect found. The shipped Linux rustic-bko is musl (stick/build-round.sh), and these commits make the musl arm newly use libc::fallocate64, fstatfs64 and statfs64. testvm/audit/rust-lint.sh lints rustic_core for every target but the two musl ones, the tests ran on glibc, and fork-tests.sh did not run at the landed head, so nothing in the report compiled rustic_core for *-linux-musl with these changes. I read libc 0.2.191 (the Cargo.lock version) on Chopin: musl/lfs64.rs has the three shims with matching signatures and musl/mod.rs has struct statfs64 with f_type: c_ulong for x86_64 and aarch64, so it should build. The Proof agent should confirm with a musl build of rustic_core at the final head.

column3: rustic_core caeed4c + aedf3c8 (G4-01 with G4-02): crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/freebsd_netbsd.rs strip_acls; crates/core/Cargo.toml version
column4: review of unit G4's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: No version gate on "absent means none" for symlink ACLs. A snapshot made before G4-02 (rel13 and older rustic-bko) or by any restic-bko never recorded a FreeBSD symlink's ACL, yet an in-place restore now strips it from the live symlink (UFS mounted acls gives every symlink under a default-ACL directory one). The ledger's G4-01 row warned against exactly this. Impact is small: nothing consults a symlink's ACL, fresh restores are unaffected, and without the strip --exact would never converge on those symlinks. Cargo.toml still says 0.14.0+backotter.1 while BACKOTTER.md calls the change .2, so new and old snapshots carry the same program_version and can never be told apart later. Already listed by the fixer as a decision for the user; the version bump should land before any snapshot is made with this code.
column10: needs-user: an in-place restore of a snapshot from before 0.14.0+backotter.2, or of restic-bko's, takes a FreeBSD symlink's own ACL off (absent is taken as none); the version is bumped (rustic_core 13517ec), so new snapshots can be told from old

column3: rustic_core 2b99ed8 + caeed4c (G4-05 with G4-01): freebsd_netbsd.rs fill_acls / strip_acls
column4: review of unit G4's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: An ACL the backup could not read is now warned about (exit 3), but the node still has no ACL attribute, so a later restore of that snapshot by root or the owner strips the file's real ACL. A restic-bko snapshot gives no warning at all for the same case (its unsupported() still swallows EPERM/EACCES), and rustic-bko treats it as BackOtter's. Consistent with how other unreadable attributes behave; the fixer listed it as a user decision. restic-bko needs the EPERM/EACCES split before cross-restore is safe here.
column10: needs-user: an ACL the backup could not read (warned, exit 3) is stripped by a later in-place restore of that snapshot; restic-bko needs the EPERM/EACCES split first

column3: rustic_core caeed4c: freebsd_netbsd.rs absent_is_unknown, restore_system_extattrs; commands/restore/exact.rs same_generic_attributes
column4: review of unit G4's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: For system extattrs the symptom is hidden rather than fixed when the node has none: a root-made snapshot of a file without system extattrs cannot say "none", so one the file gains later stays, and --exact no longer counts it. The ledger allowed this alternative and BACKOTTER.md documents it, but --exact then reports a match that is not exact. Extras are removed only when the node holds at least one system extattr.

column4: review of unit G5's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: The fix is a size cap on the user's data, and it loses attributes that restored correctly before. Seen by reading the code; not run on a guest. Before, an illumos named attribute or SMB alternate data stream of any size that fit in memory (say 20-500 MiB) was backed up and restored. Now anything over 16 MiB is left out of the snapshot (warning, counted incomplete). Any later restore over the live tree, plain or --exact, then deletes it from the file with no message at restore time: set_xattrs removes every name the node lacks, and on Haiku plan().remove does the same for a typed attribute over the cap. Side effect: the node still holds the attribute's illumos.xattr_meta entry (fill_xattr_meta only stats it), so after the removal --exact never matches that file again and resets its metadata on every run. This conflicts with the user's restore-fidelity rule of 2026-11-22, which names size caps as hardening that must not change the restored system. The fixer itself reported the limit as its own choice. Needs a refix or a user decision. Options: a cap only where the value could never be stored (near the 4 GiB blob limit, or by available memory); or keep 16 MiB but record the names left out by size in an optional generic attribute so a restore leaves them on the file and --exact ignores their xattr_meta entry (rule 4 holds: readers ignore unknown attributes). restic-bko has no cap, so the two tools' nodes also differ above 16 MiB.

column6: G6-01's stated goal, 'the next restore writes it', does not hold for a restore not run as root when the node's mode has no owner write bit (0444, 0555, 0000). Run 1 fails a write (say ENOSPC on a new file), the metadata pass then chmods the file to the node's mode, and run 2 gets EACCES in set_length/open_for_write, so it reports 'contents not restored' and exits 1 on every re-run until the user chmods or removes the file. It is loud, not silent, and root is unaffected (restricting flags are cleared before the rewrite). The underlying gap is older than this commit and in upstream's code: LocalDestination::set_length does not reset permissions and retry, as restic's file writer does on access denied. The integration test hides it: its snapshot's files are 0644 and it chmods to 0644 between the runs. From reading the code only; not run. Possible fix: leave the mode (or at least owner write) off a contents-failed file when not root, or retry the open after chmod u+w on a file the user owns.

column4: review of unit G7's fixes (read-only, High)
column6: The remove_tree half of the fix does not do what the commit says. It puts `filter_entry(|e| !walkdir::is_short_path_dir(e.path()))` on a `WalkDir ... contents_first(true)` walk. With contents_first a directory is yielded AFTER its contents (walkdir's own doc: filter_entry is then no different from Iterator::filter), so: (a) the links inside the links' directory (`0`, `1`, ...) are yielded first, pass the predicate (their names don't start with .bko-longpath-) and are removed by remove_extra; only the then-empty directory is kept. The restore still gets the files only because link_to's new readlink check remakes every link afterwards; the comment 'it stays' and the commit text 'remove_tree leaves it' are untrue. (b) When the deferred links' directory is finally yielded and rejected, FilterEntry::next calls skip_current_dir(), which at that point pops the PARENT's listing ($TMPDIR): every sibling of the links' directory that readdir returns after it is silently skipped, neither removed nor counted in `failed`/`removed`. The error text '{failed} entries not removed ...; {removed} removed' is then wrong and extra entries --delete should remove stay. Reproduced on Chopin (kernel 7.2.12) with an integration test binary built from a tree holding these commits (/bkoscratch/forkaudit-g4fix-chopin/target/debug/deps/integration-60bdb5eb4812fd56, executed read-only): TMPDIR on tmpfs passes, TMPDIR on XFS (/var/tmp) leaves `keep` in $TMPDIR. The S1 itself (silent loss of files past PATH_MAX) does stay fixed in both runs, thanks to remake and to the plan-walk skip at line 638, which is correct (not contents_first). Needed: no filter_entry on a contents_first walk; skip, with a plain `continue` and no skip_current_dir, any entry that is the links' directory or whose parent is (the parent's rmdir then fails with ENOTEMPTY as intended). Same root cause in remove_unexpected's Aliases branch: remove_tree(<links' dir>) as walk root removes all links and returns Ok(()).

On ext4 it would depend on the name hash, so on the PID. So `cargo test` with TMPDIR on a disk file system has a new fork-only failure, and fork-tests.sh only stays green because of its tmpfs TMPDIR. The test also never checks that the links are still in the links' directory right after remove_tree ran (it only checks entry types after links were remade), so it cannot see defect (a) above. Needed with the code fix: siblings of the links' directory on both sides of it in listing order (or assert independent of order), an assert that the links survive the removal, and a run with TMPDIR on XFS as well as tmpfs.

So `--clone-from PATH=DEST/../seed` (or relative `target/../old` with destination `target`) is now refused as "inside the restore's destination" although it is outside; before this commit it worked. A symlink inside DEST that points outside is refused the same way, which is defensible. bko-holt never writes such paths (holt/src/load/commands.rs:3607 builds `{top}/{sub}` with no `..`, and shared.rs restores a snapshot with a mounted subvolume nested in it as a full copy), so only hand-written rustic calls are affected. Found by reading the code, not run.

column6: The new `private` write flag (Cmd::private, commands.rs:85-89, used for LILO's lilo.conf copy at commands.rs:6156) hides the file's text only in the JSON plan document (plan.rs:451 render(..., true)). Everywhere else the full heredoc is still printed: run_cmd logs `c.shell()` before writing (exec.rs:30), the dry run of every writing stage appends `c.shell()` (exec.rs:117), and the text plan uses render(..., false) (plan.rs:438). The copy carries lilo.conf's items verbatim, password= included (the dump keeps them: boot.rs:1794/1807 `options` via lilo_list, with no redaction in redact.rs).
column7: Slackware layout whose /etc/lilo.conf has `password=s3cret` (no `password=""`). `bko-holt load L --through boot` without --commit prints `cat > /mnt/bko-target/etc/lilo.conf.bko-holt <<'EOF' ... password=s3cret` on stdout. With --commit the same text goes into RUN_DIR/log/load.log, which boot copies to the restored /var/log/bko-holt/ (commands.rs:4463) and which `bko-holt report-bug` puts in its bundle (bugreport.rs:504-513, last 3000 lines; learn_text pseudonymises identifiers, not passwords), as it also does with the unelided text plan (bugreport.rs 'plan for that run', via load::run). The file itself is written 0600, so the one place the flag protects is the one that already had root-only access.
column8: In exec.rs log and print `c.shell_elided()` at 30 and 117 (the write itself still uses c.stdin); make plan.rs:438's text plan elide too, or document why it doesn't. Separately (boot.rs/redact.rs owners) drop or scrub `password=` from boot.lilo.options in the dump and bug reports. Tests: exec::run dry run on a LILO layout with password=s3cret, assert !out.contains("s3cret") and the `# (N bytes, private: not shown)` line; run_cmd with a temp log File on a .private() write, assert the log lacks the text; a bugreport test on the same layout.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed as a privacy leak, but the anchor and fix are partly wrong. In text mode, exec.rs:30/117 and plan.rs:438 printing the full heredoc is what holt-json.md asks for. Rule 7 ('The log') elides private text only under --json. RT10f, which builds that log elision, has not landed at 689904e. J18/the golden rule keep text mode's plan.txt byte for byte. So eliding stdout or the text-mode log goes against the spec as written. The real leak is report-bug, and it contradicts holt-json.md:1401 ('neither carries it into a report'). bugreport.rs:533-557 puts the unelided text plan in (load::run -> render(..., false)). bugreport.rs:503-513 adds load.log and /var/log/bko-holt, where learn_text pseudonymises identifiers only. bugreport.rs:574 also adds the layout itself as Body::Json, and its boot.lilo options keep `password=s3cret` verbatim: boot.rs lilo_list/lilo_conf_json, with nothing for it in redact.rs or slim(). That last path predates c4917fc (lilo_list is there) and is a pre-existing hole the H5 redact audit missed. So password=s3cret reaches a public GitHub issue by default three ways. Fix first in redact/bugreport: scrub password= values in boot.lilo options and in the text and logs. Elide the report's plan with render(..., true) or shell_elided. Then decide whether text-mode stdout/log should change, which is a spec change. Test: report-bug on a LILO layout with password=s3cret must not contain s3cret. changes_output stays true.

column4: 2 RA5 S1 (wrong result on real input; H6-01's close half); Linux proc_pid_mountinfo(5) (space, tab, newline and backslash in mount points are written as \040 \011 \012 \134); RA4 item 8
column6: close()'s new slow path for a target that needs quoting (taken when shell_quote(t) != t, 5542) matches the raw target against /proc/*/mountinfo: `grep -Fq -- "$t"` (5571) and awk's `m == t` / `index(m, t)` on $5 (5564/5566). mountinfo octal-escapes exactly the bytes that make shell_quote quote (whitespace, backslash), so for those targets nothing ever matches, and an escaped $5 would also be passed unescaped-wrong to `umount "$m"`. The script exits 0 having unmounted nothing. The new test shell_heredoc_and_hostile_targets_are_quoted (8531-8553) only checks that the raw string is absent and `sh -n` passes, so it can't see this. Sibling: qubes.rs:149 os_prober_off's `grep -q ' {p} ' /proc/self/mountinfo` has the same blind spot.
column7: `bko-holt load L --target '/mnt/new root' --repo R ... --through close --commit` on a Linux LUKS/LVM/ZFS layout while systemd-udevd or logind holds a private copy of the mounts (the case the sweep exists for). mountinfo shows `/mnt/new\040root`; `grep -F '/mnt/new root'` fails for every pid, the nsfs loop's `at` prints nothing, so no namespace copy is unmounted; the closers then fail (`cryptsetup close` / `vgchange -an` / `zpool export`: device busy) and close stops. A target with only `'`, `$` or `(` works, because mountinfo doesn't escape those.
column8: Match the escaped form: build te = mountinfo_escape(t) in Rust (\\ -> \134, space -> \040, tab -> \011, newline -> \012) and pass it as T for grep/awk, unescaping m before umount (awk gsub of the four sequences, or printf '%b'). Better, move the sweep into Rust beside umount-tree (umounttree.rs already reads and unescapes mountinfo), e.g. `bko-holt umount-ns T`, and drop the two sh variants. Same for qubes.rs:149. Test: feed a mountinfo fixture with `/mnt/new\040root/boot` to the at() function under sh (or to the Rust helper) and assert it yields `/mnt/new root/boot`; extend the hostile-target test to run close's script against fake nsenter/readlink with such a fixture.
column9: confirmed: The trace holds. shell_quote (mod.rs:616) quotes space, tab, newline and backslash, which mountinfo writes as \040/\011/\012/\134; umounttree.rs's own fixture shows `my\040dir`. The slow path's `grep -Fq -- "$t"` (5571) and awk's m == t / index(m, t) on $5 (5564/5566) compare against the raw target, so no foreign-namespace copy is ever found or unmounted. A target with only ' $ ( works. Downgraded to S2: the result is not silent. Nothing goes wrong unless another namespace holds the mounts, and then the closers (cryptsetup close / vgchange -an / zpool export) fail loudly with 'busy' and the close stage exits non-zero. Whitespace in --target is also unusual; the default is /mnt/bko-target. The qubes.rs:149 sibling (os_prober_off's `grep -q ' {p} '`) is real, but there the later umount --recursive of the target still takes the bind. The fix and test sketch are right; moving the sweep beside umount-tree, which already unescapes, is the better one.

column4: 3 RA4 item 3 / Book ch.9 (bad input gives a usable error, not a dead end); RA4 item 6 (one rule, one place)
column6: A crypttab key path with a `..` component is refused twice with contradictory advice. Without --key-file, luks() (1797) and restored_key_files (4607) raise key_file_unrestorable, telling the user to give --key-file NAME=FILE, because restorable_key_file (193) calls safe_target_subpath (186), which rejects any `..`. With --key-file given, restored_key_files' given-key branch raises `crypttab key file "..." isn't a path under the target` (4593) and the plan is refused anyway. No input gets past it. A `..` that stays inside the tree is lexically harmless and is not 'on another device'.
column7: crypttab `cryptdata UUID=... /etc/keys/../data.key luks`. `bko-holt load L` reports 'crypttab's key "/etc/keys/../data.key" isn't a file the restore brings back ... give --key-file cryptdata=FILE'; rerun with `--key-file cryptdata=/tmp/k` now reports 'cryptdata: crypttab key file "/etc/keys/../data.key" isn't a path under the target'. Exit 4 both times.
column8: Normalise the key path lexically (drop `.`, resolve `..`, refuse only if it climbs above /) and use the result for `{t}{k}`. Or, with --key-file given, skip the extra keyslot and add a note instead of a problem. Either way the message must not send the user to an option that can't help. Test: luks + restored_key_files on a layout with that crypttab line, with and without --key-file: no problem with it given, and the luksAddKey/test line names `{t}/etc/data.key`.
column9: confirmed: Verified. restorable_key_file (193) uses safe_target_subpath (186), which rejects any `..` component. Without --key-file, luks() (1794-1797) and restored_key_files (4607) raise needs_key_file, whose text says 'give --key-file NAME=FILE'. With --key-file given, restored_key_files' branch (4589-4594) passes the ':'/relative/dev checks, then fails safe_target_subpath and raises "isn't a path under the target". The user is told to use an option that cannot help. All of this code is new since c4917fc. One caution on the fix: lexical `..` resolution can differ from physical resolution when a component is a symlink in the restored tree. The simpler fix is the second one: with --key-file given, skip the extra keyslot with a note instead of a problem.

column4: 2 RA4 item 2 (integer arithmetic on input checked); Book ch.9
column6: efi_prefix computes the module start as p = raw + off with checked_add (81), but never checks p <= end. module_prefix then does an unchecked `p + 8 <= end` (89). With an offset near usize::MAX this overflows. A debug build (cargo test, the farm) panics; a release build (no overflow-checks in Cargo.toml) wraps, and is only saved because u32_at's checked_add returns None. Also `raw as usize + raw_size as usize` (71) is unchecked, which matters on the 32-bit targets the cfgs admit (sys.rs has target_pointer_width branches). The bytes are a restored ESP file from the backup (the image and, if same_as, the fallback loader).
column7: A PE whose `mods` section starts with `mimg`, with a 64-bit module-info offset field of 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFF0 - raw and a valid size: efi_prefix -> module_prefix(b, usize::MAX-15, end); `p + 8` overflows: 'attempt to add with overflow' panic in debug. In release it returns Ok(None), 'no GRUB prefix', by accident.
column8: After computing p: `if p > end { return Err("the modules' offset is past the mods section".into()) }`, and write the loop as `while p.checked_add(8).is_some_and(|q| q <= end)`; use checked_add at 71 too. Test (D9): in grubprefix tests, take image(Some(..), 24, true), overwrite the module-info offset with u64::MAX - 8 (and a 32-bit image's with u32::MAX), assert efi_prefix is Err and doesn't panic.
column9: confirmed: grubprefix.rs is new since c4917fc. p = raw.checked_add(off) (81) is checked, but nothing bounds p by end, and module_prefix's `while p + 8 <= end` (89) is unchecked. With off near u64::MAX - raw, a debug build (cargo test) panics with an add overflow. A release build (Cargo.toml [profile.release] has no overflow-checks) wraps, u32_at's checked_add/get then returns None and breaks, giving Ok(None) by accident, as described. The input is a restored ESP file read by `bko-holt grub-prefix` (main.rs:105 -> grubprefix::main/plan). The same class as H6-08 (S2). The 32-bit point at line 71 is weak, since the shipped targets are 64-bit, but harmless to fix.

column4: 2 Checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); holt-json.md 'writes (J19)': which stages would make something anew on the target, as exec would run them
column6: JsonFacts.writes, the plan document's disks[].target.writes, decides by string matching whether an assemble or format command touches a target. touches() (256) passes each argv word to names_node (246). When the plan has more than one target, any command that names a stacked device gets no target, so the stage is left off. Examples: mkfs on /dev/md/0, /dev/mapper/NAME, /dev/VG/LV, and zfs create. names_node also over-matches. After a node that ends in a digit it accepts any digit, and after any node it accepts one lowercase letter. So nvme0n1 matches /dev/nvme0n10p1, ada1 matches /dev/ada10p1, c3t0d0 matches /dev/dsk/c3t0d01s1 and sda matches /dev/sdab. That is the prefix class vdev_on_targets fixed in this same change set (its doc: 'sdaa1 isn't on sda').
column7: Under-report case. A two-disk layout: md RAID1 /dev/md/0 over vda1+vdb1 holding ext4 /, with --map vda=vdb --map vdb=vdc --json. assemble's mdadm --create names /dev/vdb1 and /dev/vdc1. format's `mkfs.ext4 ... /dev/md/0` names neither, so `one` is false and touches() returns false for both targets. writes is ["partition","assemble"] for each, with no "format". The same happens with LUKS (format runs mkfs on /dev/mapper/cryptroot) or LVM (/dev/vg0/root) on a two-disk layout. In a resumed run where status shows partition and assemble Done and format not done, writes is [] for both targets, yet format's mkfs runs on them. Over-report case. Targets nvme0n1 and nvme0n10: names_node("/dev/nvme0n10p1", "nvme0n1") is true, because rest is "0p1" and starts with a digit. nvme0n1's writes then lists stages that touch only nvme0n10. The erase gate and will_erase are computed separately, so this is a wrong field rather than a wrong wipe. It is still the list Review shows as 'made anew'.
column8: Work out the per-target set from the builder's own device graph, not from argv text. For each assemble or format Cmd, take the source devices it creates on (the builder's item inputs, or Names.made reversed). Walk layout.slaves down to the source disks, then use mapping.pairs to get the targets. A Cmd that builds no device for a known target should count for every target its device stacks on. Make names_node exact, as vdev_on_targets is. When node ends in a digit, rest must be empty, a 'p' or 's' followed by digits, or one BSD partition letter. When node ends in a letter, rest may start with a digit. Tests: a jsonout test with a two-disk md RAID1 layout, and one with LUKS on vda plus plain vdb. Both must assert "format" in each target's writes. A names_node unit table must assert false for ("/dev/nvme0n10p1","nvme0n1"), ("/dev/ada10p1","ada1"), ("/dev/dsk/c3t0d01s1","c3t0d0") and ("/dev/sdab","sda"), and true for ("/dev/sd0a","sd0"), ("/dev/vtbd0p3.eli","vtbd0") and ("/dev/sda1","sda").
column9: confirmed: Verified at plan.rs:244-262 and 405-430. When mapping.pairs.len() > 1, touches() credits a stage to a target only if some argv or write word passes names_node for that node. A format mkfs on /dev/md/0, /dev/mapper/X or /dev/VG/LV, or a zfs create, names no target, so the stage gets no target and 'format' is left out of every target's writes. That is the normal two-disk md RAID1 / LUKS / LVM layout. The only writes test (jsonout.rs:937) is single-target, which takes the `one` shortcut. The over-match is real too. names_node("/dev/nvme0n10p1","nvme0n1") strips to rest "0p1", which starts with a digit, so it returns true. sda vs sdab gets through the one-lowercase-letter arm. holt-json.md:617-621 defines writes as 'which stages would make something anew on it ... as exec would run them', and Review shows it, so this is a wrong result on real input. Not in the ledger. The remake_after_restore gate doesn't use touches yet (code only in codes.rs), so there is no further impact today.

column4: Privacy (RA5 S1); holt-json.md Principle 4 ('Secrets never travel in the protocol ... in a document ... a repository URL with a password refused') and its `args` text ('never reaches args, the log or last-load.json')
column6: Under --json, a --repo URL that holds a password becomes the repo_has_password problem (plan.rs:271), but nothing keeps the URL out of what is written next. The plan document is still written. Its `args` (jsonout.rs:707-714) carry opts.argv verbatim. Its `stages` carry the restore command's argv (--repository URL), and its `text` carries the text plan, which shows the URL too. load::main (mod.rs:489) then calls record_load_run with the raw args, which writes them to RUN_DIR/last-load.json (bugreport.rs:251). So the 'refused' secret reaches the very places the spec says it never reaches. Bug reports replace repositories (redact Kind::Secret), so it doesn't leave the machine. It does reach bko-rescue's Review screen, which shows `args`, and the RAM file.
column7: `bko-holt load l.json --map vda=vdb --repo rest:https://me:pw@nas:8000/r --password-file /k/0 --json` exits 4 with problem repo_has_password. Standard output's document contains "rest:https://me:pw@nas:8000/r" in args[], in stages[restore].commands[].argv and in text. /run/bko-holt/last-load.json's args holds the same string. The test keys_and_their_files (jsonout.rs:1164-1167) checks only the problem code.
column8: When repo_has_password holds under --json, mask the userinfo password in everything the run writes out. That means the doc's args, the argv of cmd_json and the rendered text: build them from an Options copy whose repo has `me:***@` and from that copy's Built. Keep plan_sha256 over the real argv; the run is refused anyway. Do the same in record_load_run, or have main pass it masked args. Alternatively, write a bko-holt-error (bad_args) and no plan document; that is a protocol change for the user to choose. Test: extend keys_and_their_files so the whole stdout line contains no "me:pw@", and add a load::main-level test that last-load.json contains no "me:pw@".
column9: confirmed: Real. plan.rs:271 only pushes RepoHasPassword. jsonout.rs:707-714 still sets args from opts.argv verbatim, and stages/text carry the restore argv. mod.rs:489 records the raw args in last-load.json. holt-json.md:588-591 promises that such a URL 'never reaches args, the log or last-load.json'. Downgraded from S1 because no one who lacked the secret gains it. The document goes back to the caller that put the URL on argv, which already sits in /proc/PID/cmdline. last-load.json is now a 0600 file in RAM (write_private_file) that text mode fills the same way. Bug reports redact repositories. The refused run writes no /var/log. That leaves a spec promise the code breaks (doc vs code, missing test), which is S2.

column8: Exclude softraid from the newline check. Either build `passphrase` from built.keys where unlock == "passphrase" && kind != "softraid", or better, give KeyAsk a field saying how its tool reads the file (bytes as they are, or first line), so the check and pass_copy share one fact. column9: refuted: The spec decides this explicitly. holt-json.md 'Secrets' rule 4 (lines 917-920) applies the newline check 'for a group whose unlock is a passphrase', and its parenthesis 'bioctl's copy adds its own' covers softraid. Rule 2 (line 908) has bko-rescue write every secret 'no trailing newline', so a protocol-conforming softraid key file is never refused. Text mode keeps pass_copy's behaviour, and the USAGE text describes text mode. So the code matches the protocol on purpose and fails closed, with no wrong result. All that is left is that the reason text ('would be part of the passphrase') is slightly inaccurate for softraid. That is wording polish that no lint names.

column4: 6 Checklist 6 (duplicated logic) and 2; holt-json.md J19 (erase gate: 'this session's partition record') and plan_sha256's 'kernel serial and WWID (as the partition record reads them from sysfs)'
column6: table_record_text reads the target's identity only from Linux's /sys/block/NODE/device/{serial,wwid}. jsonout::kernel_identity (jsonout.rs:261-267) is the new copy of that closure, and it already knows that off Linux these must come from the scan (t.b.serial and t.b.wwid). The record wasn't changed to match. On FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, illumos and Haiku, every partition record says `serial= wwid=`, so load_wrote (592-593) binds a target by node name and size alone. The new erase gate (erase_gate, 874) and partition_counts_done now trust that record to tell 'load wrote this disk' from 'the old system's disk'.
column7: On FreeBSD, the partition stage writes the layout's table to a blank new disk ada1 and records it. In the same session, the new disk is pulled and the source's own old disk, the same size, goes into the same port, so it is ada1 again. It carries the layout's UUIDs, so is_ours is true and check_target raises no not_blank. erase_gate: t isn't blank, it isn't named in --erase, and load_wrote compares the record text, which is identical (same hostname, source, node, size, empty serial and wwid). So the gate passes without --erase. partition_counts_done is then true, because the old disk has the source's table. The --json plan raises no erase_required and the later stages run over the old system, which is the case J19 exists to stop. On Linux the record changes because sysfs gives the new disk's serial or WWID.
column8: Have one function for a target's kernel identity, kernel_identity moved to target.rs: sysfs on Linux, the scan's serial and wwid elsewhere. Use it in table_record_text and in plan_sha256. Test: a target.rs test with a non-Linux Family Sys (or by calling the identity function with the family): two TargetDisks with the same node and size but different scan serials give different table_record_text, so load_wrote fails for the swapped disk and erase_gate raises erase_required.
column9: confirmed: Verified. table_record_text (target.rs:559-570) reads only /sys/block/NODE/device/{serial,wwid}, so off Linux the record always carries 'serial= wwid='. jsonout::kernel_identity (257-265) is a second copy of that closure that already falls back to the scan's t.b.serial/wwid when Family::current() is set, and its doc claims to match the record, which it doesn't off Linux. That is real duplicated logic that has drifted. The new erase_gate (874) and partition_counts_done (607) rely on load_wrote. On BSD/illumos/Haiku they cannot tell a same-node, same-size disk swapped in mid-session (for example a USB target re-plugged as da0). table_record_text itself is unchanged since c4917fc, and its doc calls a mid-restore hot-swap unsupported, which narrows the impact. So S2 is right, not S1. Not in the ledger.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); holt-json.md 'No prompts under --json' and the keys' `unlock` table (temporary = 'nothing to ask')
column6: A GELI provider keyed by both a passphrase and a key file (keyed_by "both") is planned under --json as needing nothing. geli_assemble's KeyAsk maps it to unlock "temporary" (452-456, the `_` arm). The KeyNeeded problem is raised only for keyed == "passphrase" (484). geli_boot then builds the /dev/tty prompt for its passphrase whatever opts.json says (648). The spec says that prompt is never built under --json.
column7: A FreeBSD source whose provider was made with a passphrase and `geli init -K /boot/geli.key` (dump: keyed_by "both", keyfiles ["/boot/geli.key"]). bko-rescue runs `bko-holt load --json` with no --key-file for it. The plan shows no key_needed, and keys[0].unlock is "temporary", so the TUI asks nothing. Assemble inits the provider with only a temporary random key (-P -K RUN_DIR/keys/SRC.key), and the whole restore runs. In boot, prompt() runs `stty -echo </dev/tty`, which fails with no controlling terminal, so `geli setkey -n 0 -K .../boot/geli.key -J ...pass` never runs. The boot stage fails after the full restore, and the closers then rm the temporary key, which is the only key the new provider has. The restored data can no longer be unlocked, and the user has to load again.
column8: In geli_assemble, give keyed "both" its passphrase question: unlock "passphrase" (or a second KeyAsk beside the temporary one). Under --json, raise KeyNeeded when geli_key(&p, 0) is None and keyed is "passphrase" or "both". In geli_boot, never push prompt() under opts.json; once the plan is refused that branch can't be reached. Test: plan(zfs_on_geli with keyed_by "both" and keyfiles ["/boot/geli.key"], ["--json"]) has a KeyNeeded problem, no command in any stage contains "/dev/tty", and keys[0].unlock == "passphrase". With --key-file NAME=F the problem goes and setkey takes -J F.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed at 689904ed5ac8. geli.rs:452-456 maps keyed "both" to unlock "temporary" through the `_` arm. The --json KeyNeeded check at 484 tests only keyed == "passphrase". The init/attach match (497-516) sends "both" to the temporary-key arm, so nothing is asked in assemble. geli_boot (637-651) then pushes prompt() for "both" whenever geli_key(&p,0) is None, and never looks at opts.json. prompt (379-388) reads /dev/tty. That breaks holt-json.md:38 ('No prompts under --json') and the unlock table at 666-667, which says temporary means 'nothing to ask'. geli_refusals (611-620) only refuses keyfile with no keyfiles, or unsafe paths, so "both" gets through. When the prompt fails, setkey never runs, and the closer rm of tmp_key leaves the new provider with only a deleted key, as the finding says. Under the TUI the prompt would at best fight the TUI's terminal. No rule wins, and this is a wrong result on real input (geli init -K plus a passphrase is a documented FreeBSD setup). The fix and test sketch hold, and changes_output is true.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); NetBSD sys/dev/dkwedge/dkwedge_gpt.c (a duplicate name gets EEXIST, then the GUID); extends H9-02
column6: The H9-02 fix, wedge_clashes, looks only for a clash between a target partition's wedge name and a wedge on a disk that isn't a target. It never checks whether two target partitions are to get the same name, on one disk or across two targets. wedge_name (42-44) also ignores the live name the dump recorded (labelled.rs:281 `wedge_name`), which for the second such partition is its GUID.
column7: A NetBSD source with two FFS GPT partitions both labelled "data" (gpt allows duplicate names), on one disk or on wd0 and wd1. On the source, the kernel named the second wedge by its GUID, and the dump records that as wedge_name. On the targets, write-table copies both names, dkctl makewedges names the first "data" and the second its GUID. But part_node gives NAME=data for both. The format stage runs newfs NAME=data twice on the first partition, the mount stage mounts it at both places, and the second partition is never formatted or restored into. wedge_clashes returns nothing, because both partitions are targets.
column8: In wedge_clashes, also push a WedgeClash problem when two entries of `wanted` have the same name (sort and compare adjacent). Or make part_node prefer the dump's recorded wedge_name where it differs from the label, and refuse only when that is ambiguous. Test: alpinebsd() with parts[2].label set to parts[0].label gives wedge_clashes(...).len() == 1, and a two-disk pair list whose disks share a label gives one problem.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed. wedge_clashes (load.rs:55-97) builds `wanted` from every target partition, then compares it only against wedges listed on disks that are not targets (the `others` filter at 79). Duplicates inside `wanted` are never checked. wedge_name (42-44) uses only label, then uuid. The dump's recorded wedge_name (labelled.rs:281) is never read in load. No other duplicate-name check exists in load (grep found only the VG, --map and --reformat duplicate checks). So two GPT entries labelled alike, on one target or on two, both get part_node NAME=<label>. dkctl makewedges gives the second one its GUID, so newfs and mount hit the first wedge twice, and the second partition is never formatted or restored. This is a gap that remains after the H9-02 fix, not a restatement of it: H9-02 covered clashes with non-target disks. GPT allows duplicate names, and the source system ran with it, so the input is real. Wrong result, data put in the wrong place: S1.

column4: 2 checklist 2/3 (wrong result; error kind lost); holt-json.md 'Disks of another size' (data_fits null when fit has no usage; cant_resize carries fit_refused's reason)
column6: In verdict(), when every percentage up to VERDICT_PCT_MAX is refused as fit_over_pct, the FitOverPct arm decides data_wont_fit or beyond_limit only by whether one_lax(v, &t, 100) is Ok. When lax is Err for any other reason, `fits` is false and the verdict says the data doesn't fit. That covers zfs_member, md member, swap, an unsupported filesystem (all refused in resize_inside after the pct check at 970), no usage (DataUnknown), and a thin pool (pool_shrink_ok isn't strict-aware, contrary to one_lax's doc). The real refusal is dropped.
column7: A source vda of 2 TB: a 512 MiB ESP, then a ~1.99 TB zfs_member partition. plan_doc's `sizes` lists a 16 GiB USB stick as a candidate. The shrink is ~99.2% of the largest, so pct 1..99 all give FitOverPct. one_lax at 100 passes the pct check, and resize_inside returns why("member"). The verdict is {verdict: data_wont_fit, data_fits: false, reason: "data"}, where the spec's answer is cant_resize with reason "member". An ext4 largest with no mount usage and no free_blocks gives data_wont_fit / data_fits false where the spec says cant_resize / no_usage / data_fits null.
column8: In the FitOverPct arm, match on `lax`. Ok(Fitted) keeps today's fits test. Err(e) classifies e[0] with the same match as below: DataWontFit gives data_wont_fit, DataUnknown gives cant_resize/no_usage with data_fits None, FitRefused gives cant_resize with its reason, and FitOverPct at 100 (shrink > the partition) gives data_wont_fit. Factor that match into one fn used by both places. Fix one_lax's doc, or make pool_shrink_ok honour `strict`. Test: verdict() on the ZFS dump above onto a 1% target gives cant_resize/member, and on an ext4-without-usage dump gives cant_resize/no_usage with data_fits None.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed at fit.rs:690-697. In one_with, the FitOverPct test (968-971) runs before resize_inside (976). So a largest partition whose shrink exceeds 99% gets FitOverPct at every pct from 1 to VERDICT_PCT_MAX (99, at line 509), and `last` holds FitOverPct. one_lax at 100 passes the pct test and then fails in resize_inside with why("member") (1137), swap (1135), fs_unsupported, or DataUnknown (1263). `lax` is then Err, `fits` is false, and the verdict is data_wont_fit with data_fits Some(false) and reason "data". The why is the over-pct text. The spec (holt-json.md:1081, 1090-1091) asks for cant_resize with fit_refused's reason, and data_fits null for no_usage. plan_doc's sizes lists small candidates beside large sources, so this is reachable (the 2 TB ZFS source against a 16 GiB stick). The cost is a wrong label and why on a disk that is refused either way, so S2, not S1. changes_output is true.

column6: other_close's quoted branch, for a target shell_quote changes, compares each listed mount point with "$t" in a shell case. FreeBSD/DragonFly's list is `mount -p | awk '{ print $2 }'` (770) and illumos's is `awk '{ print $2 }' /etc/mnttab` (768). Both split on blanks, so a mount point containing a space never comes out whole. NetBSD/OpenBSD's sed list (769) does. This predates the fix (the awk program compared the same cut lines), but H9-04's fix made such a target a supported case.
column7: `bko-holt load ... --target "/mnt/new disk"` on a FreeBSD UFS source. The mount stage mounts at '/mnt/new disk' (quoted) and the restore runs. In close, `mount -p | awk '{print $2}'` prints "/mnt/new" (or "/mnt/new\040disk" where mount -p escapes it), which matches neither "$t" nor "$t"/*. The loop unmounts nothing and exits 0, so load reports the close done with the restored filesystems still mounted. Pulling the disk then leaves dirty UFS. On illumos the same happens with /etc/mnttab, which is tab-separated.
column8: List mount points whole. On illumos use `awk -F'\t' '{ print $2 }' /etc/mnttab`. On FreeBSD/DragonFly, parse `mount` with the sed form NetBSD uses (`s/^.* on \(.*\) (.*/\1/p`), or decode \040 from mount -p. Or refuse a --target containing whitespace for these families at parse time. Test: run the built close script with fake `mount -p` and `umount` on PATH (as qubes' scripts_quote_a_hostile_target does), and assert umount receives '/mnt/new disk'.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed at load.rs:768-781. For a target that shell_quote changes, the case compares each line of `list` with "$t". The illumos list (768) and the FreeBSD/DragonFly list (770) use awk's default field splitting, so a mount point with a blank comes out cut ("/mnt/new") or, where escaped, as \040. Neither matches "$t" or "$t"/*. The loop unmounts nothing and exits 0. --target only has to be absolute and not / (mod.rs:374-377), and the H9-04 fix (efa74ce) made a spaced target a supported, quoted case. This is a residual H9-04's fix did not cover: H9-04 was about quoting, and this is the parsing of the mount list. It is not already in the ledger. With GELI or ZFS, the closers (geli detach, export) may then fail visibly, but for plain UFS the close reports done with the tree still mounted. A non-default target makes this rare: S2 stands.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (wrong result); holt-json.md fit_pct ('for a bigger one, the percentage that would use the whole extra')
column6: verdict()'s bigger loop stops at the first percentage whose outcome has no partition change (`d.part.is_none() => break`). one() gives that for three reasons (956-967): an MBR entry that can't reach further, under 1 MiB of room, or `pct`% of the largest under 1 MiB. The last one depends on pct, so a higher percentage may still grow it.
column7: A dump whose largest partition is 80 MiB, onto a target ~20 MiB bigger. At pct 1, cap = 80 MiB*1% rounds down to 0 MiB, grow is 0, and one() returns Fitted with part None. The loop breaks and the verdict is bigger with fit_pct null. At about pct 24, cap reaches the ~19 MiB of room and unused_bytes is 0, which is the fit_pct the spec asks for. This is only reachable for a largest partition under 100 MiB with an extra of at most half of it, so real input is rare.
column8: Treat `Fitted` with part None as "not this percentage" (`=> {}`) instead of break: the loop is bounded by FIT_MAX, and the MBR and no-room cases give None at every pct anyway. Test: verdict() on a GPT dump with one 80 MiB ext4 partition onto a disk 20 MiB bigger gives fit_pct Some(n) with n <= FIT_MAX and change_pct > 0.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed. In the bigger loop (fit.rs:614-626), `Fitted(d) if d.part.is_none() => break` fires at pct 1 whenever cap = big.sectors*pct/100/mib*mib < 1 MiB, that is, a largest partition under 100 MiB (one_with 932 and 955-967). That case depends on pct, unlike the MBR-reach and under-1-MiB-room cases. For an 80 MiB largest and about 20 MiB extra, pct around 24 gives grow equal to room and unused_bytes 0. Today the verdict has fit_pct null where the spec (holt-json.md fit_pct) asks for the percentage. Replacing break with `{}` is safe: the other two None cases give None at every pct, and the loop is bounded by FIT_MAX. Real input is rare (small disks or sticks), so this is a wrong result of low reach: S2. changes_output is true.

column4: RA5 S1 (privacy leak); checklist 2/8; bugreport USAGE (bugreport.rs:44-53) promises user names 'from /home paths ... in the dump, the logs and the error output alike'
column6: Collector::scan only learns a user from '/home/NAME' when the character before '/home/' is not alphanumeric and not one of '/_-.'. The rule exists to skip DragonFly's /usr/obj/home/USER, but it also skips the home paths of supported systems: '/var/home/NAME' (Fedora Silverblue/Kinoite/Bazzite, ostree, where /home is a symlink to var/home) and '/usr/home/NAME' (FreeBSD 13 and older, where /home is a symlink to usr/home). H5-01 added learn_text and H5-02 gave the substitution Edge::Right. That redacts '/var/home/bob' only once 'bob' has been learned somewhere else. On these systems a user's name is usually nowhere else in the dump, so it is never learned.
column7: Kinoite or Bazzite (guest kinoite44 in 1F) with user bob and no separate /home mount. `restic-bko backup / 2> errs.txt` writes `error: lstat /var/home/bob/.cache/x: permission denied`. Then `bko-holt report-bug --stderr errs.txt`: learn_text -> scan reaches '/home/' with before='r', skips it, and 'bob' is never learned. The public report keeps '/var/home/bob/.cache/x' verbatim, against USAGE's promise. The same happens with load's log, last-load.json's cwd (/var/home/bob) and the layout path. FreeBSD 13's `/usr/home/bob/...` leaks the same way.
column8: In scan, accept '/home/' when the text before it is exactly '/var' or '/usr' (with '/var' or '/usr' starting a path: at the start or after a non-path character). Keep refusing every other prefix, including '/usr/obj/home/' (DragonFly). Tests: (a) a redact.rs unit test: Collector::learn_text on 'lstat /var/home/bob/x' and '/usr/home/carol/y' learns bob and carol, and '/usr/obj/home/builder/sys' learns nothing; (b) a variant of bugreport identifiers_only_in_free_text with a --stderr file holding '/var/home/bob/...' and a cwd of /usr/home/carol, asserting that neither name is in b.text.
column9: confirmed: At redact.rs:638-641 in the snapshot, scan skips '/home/' when the character before it is alphanumeric or one of '/_-.'. For '/var/home/bob' and '/usr/home/bob' that character is 'r', so the path is skipped. scan is the only place that learns Kind::User (line 647). Neither learn() nor walk() learns it any other way. The Edge::Right sub at 972 works only once the name has been learned. On Kinoite/Bazzite the dump has /var/home only as a mount target, with no user part, so in the --stderr text, the logs and the cwd (bugreport.rs:441-443, 499-522) 'bob' is never learned and stays verbatim. That breaks USAGE 44-47. The case is not in the ledger: H5-01 and H5-02 cover learn_text and the edge, not this prefix rule. The DragonFly test at 1869 shows the fix has to keep /usr/obj/home refused, as the finding says.

column4: checklist 2/3 (no hang on real input); the module's own reasoning at sys.rs:409-413 ('a hung NFS or FUSE mount can't hang the dump')
column6: build_with calls sys.statvfs(&m.target) for every layout mount. On 64-bit Linux, holt's main platform, that is a direct libc statvfs(2) call with no time limit. is_layout_mount (mounts.rs:70) keeps nfs, nfs4, cifs and fuse.* mounts (PSEUDO doesn't list them), so a hard NFS mount to a dead server, or a hung FUSE daemon, blocks `bko-holt dump` forever. a9de440 moved the other cfg (32-bit Linux and everything not Linux-64) to `df -Pk` through the timed runner. Its doc gives exactly this hazard as the reason, but the 64-bit path is left exposed.
column7: A 64-bit Linux source with `server:/export /mnt/nfs nfs4 hard` whose server is unreachable. `bko-holt dump` reaches mounts_json, statvfs("/mnt/nfs") sleeps in the kernel (TASK_KILLABLE), and the dump never finishes or prints anything. The same happens with report-bug, which builds a dump of the system.
column8: Give the in-process call a time limit, the way RealRunner does for commands: run statvfs on a spawned thread, wait with mpsc recv_timeout (the runner's timeout), and on timeout return None plus a sys.warn naming the mount (the thread is left behind, as exec_status leaves a stuck child). A healthy system's output doesn't change. Test: put the per-mount usage call behind a function that takes the usage provider and a limit; a unit test with a provider that sleeps past the limit asserts that the call returns None and a warning within the limit plus a margin.
column9: confirmed: report.rs:1514 calls sys.statvfs(&m.target) for every is_layout_mount mount. PSEUDO (mounts.rs:63-67) does not list nfs, nfs4, cifs or fuse.* (other than gvfsd, portal and lxcfs), so those mounts are kept. On 64-bit Linux, sys.rs:397-400 calls libc statvfs directly with no time limit (sys.rs:512-553). The df_usage doc at 409-413 gives exactly this hang as the reason for using the timed runner, but only the other cfg uses it. A hard mount to a dead server blocks the statvfs, so the dump never finishes. The ledger rows on statvfs, H1-08 and H1-15, cover the struct comments and the API shape, not this hang. A hang is not one of RA5's S1 kinds, so S2 stands.

column6: write_report's comment says create_new 'also refuses a symlink in PATH's last place'. That holds only for the dry run. Otherwise an AlreadyExists (which a symlink at PATH gives) falls back to OpenOptions::write+truncate, which follows the link. f.metadata() then stats the target, and a regular-file target is truncated, filled with the report and chmodded 0600. The chmod is new in this change; std::fs::write before it only truncated. The comment at line 295 ('Someone else's file ... it keeps its mode') contradicts the next line, which sets 0600, and the doc above it.
column7: In a shared directory where symlinks are followed (a group-writable dir, a BSD /tmp, or Linux with fs.protected_symlinks=0), another user plants bko-report-20261124-101500.txt -> /etc/passwd, a predictable default name. root runs `sudo bko-holt report-bug` there at that second. /etc/passwd is truncated, holds the report, and is mode 0600, so non-root logins break. Even without an attacker, `-o notes.txt` where notes.txt is a symlink to a shared 0644 file silently makes that file 0600.
column8: Before the fallback open, take symlink_metadata(path). If it is a symlink whose target is a regular file, refuse with an error saying so. A symlink to a non-regular file (/dev/stdout -> /proc/self/fd/1) is still written to as it is. After opening, compare the (dev, ino) of f.metadata() with metadata(path) so that a swap between the two calls is refused. Fix the comment at 295. Test: extend write_report_is_private with a Tree symlink 'link.txt' -> a 0644 file holding 'keep': write_report returns Err, and the file still holds 'keep' with mode 0644; write_report("/dev/stdout") still succeeds.
column9: confirmed: bugreport.rs:290-292: when create_new gets AlreadyExists (which a symlink at PATH also gives), the code falls back to OpenOptions write+truncate. That open follows the link. f.metadata() then stats the target, and for a regular-file target 296 sets 0600. The comment at 295 ('it keeps its mode') contradicts 296 and the fn doc at 278-279. The 288 comment's 'refuses a symlink' is true only of the O_EXCL step. The default name (line 139) is predictable to the second. One correction: the old std::fs::write (a9de440) already followed the link and truncated, so the symlink-follow is older. What is new is only the chmod 0600 of the target. Making an existing regular file 0600 is documented as intended, but doing it through a symlink is not, and the stale comment is real. S2 is right, and changes_output=true fits the proposed refusal. This is not H5-03, which is about last-load.json.

column4: checklist 2 (wrong result on input); D9 corrupted-input tests
column6: In the native nvlist's string-array branch (type 17), the cursor moves on by the length of cstr_until's String, which is String::from_utf8_lossy of the raw bytes, not by the raw byte count. One invalid UTF-8 byte becomes U+FFFD (3 bytes), so p overshoots by 2 for each such byte, and every later element in the array is read from the wrong offset. The bounds checks keep it from panicking, but the result is wrong. The hunk was rewritten in dd8ded1 and kept `p += s.len() + 1`.
column7: A native-encoded nvlist (zpool.cache, as real_zpool_cache_native_encoding reads) holding a string array ["a\xffb", "cd"]. The raw layout is 'a\xffb\0cd\0'. The first element decodes as "a\u{FFFD}b" (5 bytes), p moves on 6 instead of 4 and lands on 'd', so the second element reads as "d" (or 'unterminated string' when it ends the pair). The dump's JSON records the wrong strings.
column8: Have cstr_until return the raw length too, e.g. Result<(String, usize), String> with the byte count before the NUL, and advance p by raw_len + 1. Test: in the existing synthetic native nvlist test (zfs.rs ~634), add a type-17 pair with an invalid UTF-8 byte in its first element, and assert that the second element decodes intact.
column9: confirmed: zfs.rs:285 does `p += s.len() + 1`, where s comes from cstr_until (170-174), which returns String::from_utf8_lossy. Each invalid byte becomes U+FFFD (3 bytes), so p overshoots by 2 per invalid byte. Later elements of the array are then read from the wrong offset, or fail with 'unterminated string' or 'nvlist truncated'. get() bounds every read, so nothing panics; the result is just wrong. Invalid UTF-8 in a type-17 string array in a real zpool.cache is rare, so this is corrupted or odd input (D9), not common real input. S2 fits better than S1. Not in the ledger.

column4: checklist 1/7 (key handling, H5 focus; doc against behaviour: 'its Drop wipes the word indices', zeroize_* 'without allowing dead-store elimination')
column6: a9de440 wipes the entropy, bit buffers and word indices in generate, from_entropy, decode and check. But every from_entropy and decode calls checksum -> bytes::sha256_hex -> sha256, and sha256 starts with `let mut msg = data.to_vec()`: a heap copy of all 128 bits of entropy, which is dropped without a wipe. sha256_hex then also allocates the hex of their hash. The recovery key's full secret is left in freed heap memory on every generate() and every check(), which defeats the wipes around it.
column7: bko-recovery-words generates a key. from_entropy(&e) -> checksum(entropy) -> sha256(entropy) allocates a 64-byte Vec holding the 16 entropy bytes, then 0x80 and the length, and frees it unwiped. A later heap reuse, a core dump or a swap-out of that page carries the exact entropy, while the code wipes its own stack copies with black_box and fences.
column8: Compute the checksum without a heap copy: for the 16-byte input, build the single padded SHA-256 block in a stack [u8; 64], hash it, take out[0] >> 4, and zeroize_bytes the block (expose a crate-internal sha256 over a fixed block, or have sha256 wipe msg before it returns). That also removes the from_str_radix/unwrap_or(0) detour through hex. Test: BIP39's test vectors (already in recovery.rs) still pass; the wipe itself is checked by review only, since no test can observe freed memory.
column9: confirmed: recovery.rs:276-279: checksum calls bytes::sha256_hex(entropy), and sha256 (bytes.rs:537-539) starts with data.to_vec(). That is a 16-byte heap copy of the full entropy. The push(0x80) at the next line reallocates, which frees the first buffer unwiped, and the padded 64-byte Vec is dropped unwiped too. The stack schedule w[0..4] also holds the entropy words and is not wiped. Every from_entropy (240-253, from generate) and every decode (258-273, from check) goes through it. That works against the zeroize_* policy and the Words doc at 76-77, which the surrounding code otherwise follows carefully. This is defence in depth, not an observable wrong result, so S2. Not in the ledger.
